Proofs as Execution Trees for the π \pi -Calculus
Matteo Acclavio, Giulia Manara

Abstract
In this paper, we establish the foundations of a novel logical framework for the π \pi -calculus, based on the deduction-as-computation paradigm. Following the standard proof-theoretic interpretation of logic programming, we represent processes as formulas, and we interpret proofs as computations. To be precise, we interpret proofs as execution trees. For this purpose, we define a cut-free sequent calculus for an extension of first-order multiplicative and additive linear logic. This extension includes a non-commutative and non-associative connective to faithfully model the prefix operator, and nominal quantifiers to represent name restriction. Finally, we design proof nets providing canonical representatives of derivations up to local rule permutations.

1
Introduction

Formal reasoning about the properties of concurrent program executions is significantly
more complex than analyzing sequential programs.
The main challenge in the concurrent setting
arises from the lack of formalisms for efficient representations
of the set of traces of a program in the presence of
interleaving
concurrency, where the mutual order of certain tasks of a program is irrelevant.
This is due to the inherent limitations of languages commonly used to represent trace
reasoning, including natural language, where it can be impossible
to describe a set of events arranged in complex patterns in a canonical way,
other than by inefficiently listing all possible total orders.
A language for optimizing the trace analysis of concurrent programs should:

1.

ignore irrelevant differences, such as the mutual order of independent events;

2.

group traces that differ only in branching caused by internal choices within the program;

3.

distinguish sets of traces that differ due to factors beyond the control of the program, such as race conditions and side effects.

In this work, we develop a formalism satisfying these three desiderata to represent execution trees of processes of the
\pi
-calculus in a canonical way, based on the
deduction-as-computation
interpretation for proofs a logic extending first-order multiplicative additive linear logic.

An approach inspired by logic programming.

In the
logic programming
paradigm,
programs are interpreted as sets of formulas,
and computation is performed by applying methods (or rules) to these formulas.
In
[
65
]
Miller et al illustrate how a
deduction-as-computation
interpretation of proof search in the sequent
calculus allows to account for program executions:
sequents correspond to snapshots of the state of the system,
and sequent rules can be interpreted as methods executing the instructions encoded
by logical connectives.

In the setting of deduction-as-computation, two forms of non-determinism appear in program executions that are not as easily observable in
other frameworks
1
1

1

In particular, within the proofs-as-processes setting that arises from the Curry-Howard isomorphism, the non-determinism resulting from an internal choice is not observable in the computations of typed processes, as the type of a process predetermines the choice.

:
the
don’t care
non-determinism, depending on the possibility of applying
rules to independent sets of formulas, and the
don’t know
non-determinism, that arises from the possibility of applying (potentially different) rules to overlapping subsets of formulas.
In the proof-search interpretation of program execution, differences in derivations caused by don’t care non-determinism are considered irrelevant, at the point that two proofs which can be transformed into one another through
rule permutation

(i.e., by exchanging the order of rules operating on disjoint sub-sequents) are usually identified.

This work aims to apply results in the study of proof equivalence
[
50
,
49
,
52
,
82
]
in the framework of deduction-as-computation to provide canonical representations of sets of traces.
In particular, we develop a syntax based on results about canonical representation of proofs to uniquely model a set of traces differing in the order of independent events, in compliance with desiderata
1
.
We focus on a deduction-as-computation interpretation of
proof nets
rather than sequent calculus derivation.

Why proof nets?

Various works
[
14
,
13
,
7
]
have already highlighted the benefits of this approach where the syntax captures interleaving concurrency by default.
Proof nets were introduced as a graphical formalism for
linear logic
proofs
[
33
]
.
They abstract away irrelevant information contained in sequent calculus derivations, such as mutual order of independent inference rules.
This syntax allows for an optimal level of abstraction for the multiplicative fragment of linear logic (
\mathsf{MLL}
), providing canonical representatives for proofs with respect to independent rule permutations, a polynomial proof translation, and a geometrical correctness criterion allowing to check in polynomial time if a graph is the encoding of a proof (making proof nets for
\mathsf{MLL}
a proof system in the sense of
[
24
]
).
However, the definition of proof nets for extensions of
\mathsf{MLL}
requires trade-offs
between canonicity, the efficiency of correctness criterion and the efficiency of normalization
procedure (see
[
41
]
for
\mathsf{MLL}
with units,

[
55
,
56
,
53
,
52
]
for multiplicative-additive linear logic
(
\mathsf{MALL}
) and
[
2
]
for multiplicative-exponential linear logic).

To provide an intuition of our approach, we show for the process
P
in

Equation

1
how we can annotate information about communications (and selections) performed during all the possible executions of
P
while ignoring inessential details such as the specific order of independent transitions.

Note that the only (don’t know) non-determinism during executions of
P
is caused by an internal choice: the branching due to the choice of a label in
L=\{\ell_{1},\ell_{2}\}
. Thus, we have a unique proof net according to the desiderata
1
and
2
.
In this representation the set of links
\{{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,0.16}\ell_{1}},{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{b}}}\}
and
\{{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,0.16}\ell_{2}},{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}{c}}}\}
are mutually exclusive – in the terminology of event structures
[
86
]
, we would say they are in conflict relation.

At the same time, our syntax still allows us to distinguish the two distinct executions of the process in
Equation

2
, as specified by desideratum
3
, which are determined by a race condition on
x
enforcing a (don’t know) non-deterministic choice during the execution.

(2)

Which proof nets?

There are different syntaxes for proof nets for
\mathsf{MALL}
, each providing a different level of abstraction and capturing different subsets of the rule permutations in the sequent calculus – rules permutations are reported in
Figure

16
.
The first syntax of proof nets for
\mathsf{MALL}
was introduced by Girard in
[
33
]
.
These are referred to as
box nets
because of the way they encode the rules for the additive conjunction
\with
. These proof nets provide polynomial time proof translation and correctness criterion. However, they are not canonical with respect to rule permutations involving the rule for
\with
.
In
[
36
]
, Girard also introduced
monomial nets
for
\mathsf{MALL}
, lacking of a polynomial time correctness criterion (but a polynomial-time proof translation), but unable to not improve the level of abstraction in the general setting.
For this reason, Hughes and Van Glabbeek introduced in
[
55
,
56
]
a new syntax of proof nets for
\mathsf{MALL}
called
slice nets
.
These proof nets capture all rule permutations in
Figure

16
while keeping a polynomial correctness criterion, but they lack of a polynomial proof translation.
The absence of a polynomial proof translation is unsurprising because each slice net can be conceived as a canonical representative of a class of derivations, which may include derivations whose sizes differ by an exponential factor.
This is due to the fact that the rule permutation between the two-premises multiplicative rule
\mathop{\otimes}
and the two-premises additive rule
\with
-rules requires to duplicate an entire subtree of the derivation (see
Figure

16
).
In order to recover a polynomial proof translation, Hughes and Heijltjes introduced
conflict nets
in
[
53
,
52
]
, which can capture only
local
rule permutations – that is, all rule permutations except the one between the
\with
and the
\mathop{\otimes}
.
This is obtained by having trees of axiom links (instead of a set of sets of axiom links as in slice nets) where axiom links are in a “multiplicative” concordance relation, or in a “additive” conflict relation.

At the same time, there are two main approaches for proof nets for first-order logic.
One is to consider the choice of witnesses for the existential quantifier (and, in our case, for the nominal quantifiers) as part of the information of a proof. This leads to the notion of what we refer to as
witness nets
(as in
[
42
]
) developed in
[
33
,
34
,
35
]
, which in
[
37
, Chapter 11]
Girard claims to be “the only really satisfactory extension of proof-nets”.
However, how explained by Hughes in
[
51
]
, having the witnesses being part of the proof leads to undesirable consequences such as the lack of canonical proofs due to the existence of infinitely many possible witnesses (possibly of exponentially larger size); for an example, consider the formula
\exists{P}.(x)\multimap\exists{P}.(x)
which has infinitely many proofs, one for each possible witness for
x
.
Moreover, the complexity of cut-eliminination becomes exponential, and requiring non-local rewriting rules even in first-order
\mathsf{MLL}
.
For this reason, in
[
51
]
Hughes introduced another approach for the design of proof nets for first-order logic, which abstracts away the choice of witnesses for the quantifiers, thus satisfying the principle of
generality
(in the sense of Lambek
[
58
]
) by identifying those proofs differing in the witness assignment.
These proof nets, called
unification nets
, were initially developed for first-order
\mathsf{MLL}
, and have been recently extended for the purely additive fragment of linear logic in by Hughes, Heijltjes and Straßburger in
[
42
]
).

In this paper we develop both conflict and slice (unification) nets for
\mathsf{PiL}
to provide canonical representatives of execution trees for the
\pi
-calculus modulo different notions of interleaving:

•

Conflict nets (
Section

5.1
) abstract away the order of independent transitions, as soon as this order does not interact with branching of the execution tree.

•

Slice nets (
Section

5.2
) abstract away the order of any independent transitions in a process, even when the execution tree branches.

In choreographic programming
[
70
]
, the distinction between these two flavors of interleaving can be easily understood in terms of restriction on the possibility of performing out-of-order instruction in the operational semantics:
while slice nets identify execution trees of the standard operational semantics, where both communications and choices can be delayed, conflict nets allow to only delay communications, and not choices.

Contributions of the Paper.

We develop a
new
logical framework (
\mathsf{PiL}
) based on an extension of first-order
multiplicative and additive linear logic (
\mathsf{MALL}^{1}
) with a

non-commutative non-associative connective
and
nominal quantifiers
,
to provide logical operators that faithfully model the high-level search instruction corresponding to the prefix composition and restriction in the
\pi
-calculus.
We define a cut-free sequent calculus in which execution trees of a process can be interpreted as derivations of the corresponding formula.

We also define two syntaxes of proof nets for
\mathsf{PiL}
by combining the techniques used in
unification nets
for first-order multiplicative linear logic
[
54
]
and first-order additive linear logic
[
42
]
,
with the techniques used in
conflict nets

[
53
,
41
]
and in
slice nets

[
56
]
for
\mathsf{MALL}
.
As a restriction of our syntax, we then define unification conflict nets and unification slice nets for first-order
\mathsf{MALL}
.

Finally, by combining the correspondence between execution trees and derivations, and between derivations modulo local rule permutations and proof nets, we provide a syntax in which we have canonical representatives of execution trees modulo interleaving.

Related Works on Processes as Formulas.

Following the ideas in
[
65
]
,
Miller proposed in
[
64
]
a theory within linear logic allowing to interpret the reduction semantics of the
\pi
-calculus as implication in the theory, where parallel is internalized by the
\invamp
and the choice operator
+
in the original formulation of the
\pi
-calculus
[
69
]
by the
\mathop{\oplus}
.
Guglielmi developed an extension of multiplicative linear logic with a non-commutative connective aiming at internalizing sequentiality in
[
38
,
39
]
, lately leading to the design
deep inference
and the formalism of the
calculus of structures

[
40
]
to obtain a satisfactory proof system for the logic
\mathsf{BV}
.
In
[
21
]
Bruscoli established a
processes-as-formulas
and
computation-as-deduction
correspondence for a simple fragment of
CCS
(without recursion, choice, and restriction) where each successful terminating execution of a process corresponds to specific derivations in
\mathsf{BV}
.
This correspondence has been extended to the
\pi
-calculus by Horne, Tiu et al.
[
45
,
46
,
48
]
, including the choice operator (
+
), modeled via the additive connective
\mathop{\oplus}
, and name restriction, modeled using
nominal quantifiers
in the spirit of
[
73
,
30
]
.
We highlight here the main differences of our approach with respect to the aforementioned works:

•

we use a non-associative non-commutative self-dual connective
\blacktriangleleft
(instead of the non-commutative but associative
\triangleleft
in
\mathsf{BV}
).
This choice allows for a cut-free sequent calculus for
\mathsf{PiL}
,
while no sequent calculus for
\mathsf{BV}
or any of its extension can exist
[
83
]
;

•

in
[
47
,
48
]
Horne et al. use
the original version of the
\pi
-calculus
[
69
]
which feature a choice operator
+
with an undesirable “non-local” behavior, which requires to forwardly check that it will entail a communication rule.
Its rule is written as follows

+:A+B\quad\to\quad A^{\prime}\qquad\mbox{only if }A\to A^{\prime}

That is, the choice operator
+
is not complitely free to choose between
A
and
B
, but it is constrained by the possibility of performing an action after such a choice. That is, if
A
cannot perform any action, then the choice
A+B
cannot reduce to
A
.

A logical operator modeling such a choice operator should have a rule capable of spotting (within a given context) the sub-formulas on which some rules can be applied.
Such a behavior, to the best of our knowledge, has never been studied in the literature of proof theory.
For this reason, we consider the version of the
\pi
-calculus from
[
85
,
32
]
in which the two choice operators play different roles:
the
label-send

x\triangleleft\left\{\ell:P_{\ell}\right\}_{\ell\in L}
allows a process to choose its continuation independently of the environment (which we model with the additive conjunction
\with
, whose rule branches a derivation duplicating the context), while the
label-receive

x\triangleright\left\{\ell:P_{\ell}\right\}_{\ell\in L}
allows a process to choose according to the environment (which we model with the additive disjunction
\mathop{\oplus}
, whose rule is applied according to the context’s need).
This latter version of the
\pi
-calculus is the one used in the literature of session types
[
85
,
32
,
44
]
and choreographic programming
[
70
]
.
2
2

2

Applications of the logical framework we develop, as well as more precise connections with session types and choreographic programming are presented in the companion paper
[
8
]
.

•

in the work of Bruscoli
[
21
]
, and in the works of Horne and Tiu
[
48
,
46
]
derivations correspond to executions, while in our work derivations represent execution trees.
In the latter works, the original Milner’s choice operator (
+
) is modelled in the system
\mathsf{MAV}
by using the additive connective
\mathop{\oplus}
from additive linear logic, since the additional information about the environment seems to be guaranteed (a-posteriori) by the fact that the correspondence is only established between successful executions and derivations.
However, undesired behaviors may still occur in establishing the correspondence executions-as-derivations in
\mathsf{MAV}
.
For an example, consider the process
A+\mathsf{Nil}\;|\;x!\langle a\rangle\;|\;x?(a).
, which is stuck, but derivable in
\mathsf{MAV}
.

Note that if we restrict the label-send constructor
x\triangleleft\left\{\ell:P_{\ell}\right\}_{\ell\in L}
on singleton sets of labels, or, equivalently, if we redesign the rule for the additive connective
\with
in such a way it only has a single premise (that is, we prune the other premise), then we can recover a correspondence between derivations and executions also in our setting.

•

as Horne and Tiu in
[
45
,
46
,
48
]
,
we use a pair of dual nominal quantifiers
(instead of a self-dual quantifier as in
[
63
,
67
,
78
]
)
to model restriction.
3
3

3

In
[
45
]
the authors report the use of a non-self-dual quantifier to model restriction was suggested them by Alessio Guglielmi in a private communication.

However, as explained in detail in
Remark

8
and in
Appendix

A
,
our pair of dual quantifiers satisfies different proof theoretical properties.

Structure of the paper.

In
Section

2
we recall standard definitions for sequent systems and syntax and semantics of the
\pi
-calculus.
In
Section

3
we present formulas and sequent systems, explaining the design choices we made in the opeartors of the logic
\mathsf{PiL}
.
In
Section

4
we study their proof theoretical properties of our system, including relevant formula equivalences and cut-elimination.
In
Section

5
we present the syntax of proof nets for
\mathsf{PiL}
, providing translations from derivations to proof nets, and from proof nets to derivations (sequentialization).
In
Section

6
we prove canonicity for our proof nets with respect to local rule permutations.
In
Section

7
we show how formulas in
\mathsf{PiL}
can be used to encode processes of the
\pi
-calculus, and how execution trees of a process
P
can be represented by derivations of the corresponding formula.
Thereby, we show that equivalent execution trees (modulo interleaving) can be represented by the same proof net.
We conclude in
Section

8
by discussing extensions of this framework and its possible applications.

2
Preliminary Notions

We assume the reader to be familiar with the notion of trees and of formula tree, as well as with the syntax of sequent calculus (see, e.g.,
[
84
]
), but we recall here the main definitions.
We may identify formulas with their formula-trees and we consider
sequents
as forests made of formula-trees.
4
4

4

Said differently, a sequent is a set of occurrences of formulas.
Note that defining a sequent as a multiset of formulas would require the introduction of additional structure to pinpoint on which occurrences of formulas rules are applied, making way more cumbersome the definition of proof nets (
Section

5
) and preventing the confluence of cut-elimination due to the impossibility of distinguishing which occurrence of formula is active for a
\mathsf{cut}
.

of formulas in a given grammar.

A
sequent rule

{\mathsf{r}}
is an expression of the form

\scriptstyle{\mathsf{r}}\;

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma

,

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma_{1}

\scriptstyle{\mathsf{r}}\;

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma

, or

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma_{1}

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma_{2}

\scriptstyle{\mathsf{r}}\;

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma

.
The sequent
\Gamma
is called
conclusion
and the sequents above the line
premises
.
An occurrence of formula in the conclusion (resp. in a premise) of a rule but in none of its premises (resp. not in its conclusion) is said
principal
(resp.
active
).
A
sequent system

\mathsf{X}
is a set of sequent rules.

A
derivation
in
\mathsf{X}
is a non-empty tree
\mathcal{D}
of sequents, whose root is called
conclusion
, such that each sequent in
\mathcal{D}
is conclusion of a rule in
\mathsf{X}
, whose children are (all and only) the premises of the rule.
An
open derivation
is a derivation whose leaves may be the conclusion of no rules, in which case are called
open premises
.
We may denote a derivation (resp. an open derivation with an open premise
\Delta
)
\mathcal{D}
with conclusion
\Gamma
by

\scriptstyle\scriptstyle\mathcal{D}\;

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma

\left(\mbox{resp. }{}\mathchoice{\hbox{$\displaystyle{{{{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}}{{{}}}\vbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\vbox{\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\vbox{\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{\kern 2.1
\pi
-Calculus

\begin{array}[]{c}\begin{array}[]{c|c}\mbox{Processes}&\mbox{Structural Equivalence}\\
\begin{array}[]{l@{\;}c@{\;}l@{\;}|@{\;}l}P,Q,R&\coloneqq&\mathsf{Nil}&\mbox{nil}\\
&|&x!\langle y\rangle.P&\mbox{send ($y$ on $x$)}\\
&|&x?(y).P&\mbox{receive ($y$ on $x$)}\\
&|&P\;|\;Q&\mbox{parallel}\\
&|&(\nu x)P&\mbox{restriction (or nu)}\\
&|&x\triangleleft\left\{\ell:P_{\ell}\right\}_{\ell\in L}&\mbox{label-send (on $x$)}\\
&|&x\triangleright\left\{\ell:P_{\ell}\right\}_{\ell\in L}&\mbox{label-receive (on $x$)}\end{array}&\begin{array}[]{r@{\;\steq\;}l}P\;\equiv&P^{\alpha}\\
P\;|\;Q\;\equiv&Q\;|\;P\\
(P\;|\;Q)\;|\;R\;\equiv&P\;|\;(Q\;|\;R)\\
(\nu x)(\nu y)P\;\equiv&(\nu y)(\nu x)P\\
P\;|\;\mathsf{Nil}\;\equiv&P\\
(\nu x)S\;\equiv&S\\
(\nu x)P\;|\;S\;\equiv&(\nu x)(P\;|\;S)\end{array}\\
\hline\cr\begin{tabular}[]{c}with $x,y\in\mathcal{N}$ and $L\subset\mathcal{L}$.
The constructors binding variables\\
are $(\nu x)P$ binding $x$ in $P$, and $x?(y).P$ binding $y$ in $P$
only\end{tabular}&\begin{tabular}[]{c}$P^{\alpha}$ $\alpha$-equivalent to $P$\\
$x$ is not a name occurring free in $S$\end{tabular}\end{array}\par\\
\hline\cr\hline\cr\begin{array}[]{c|c}\lx@intercol\hfil\text{Reduction Semantics}\hfil\lx@intercol\\
\begin{array}[]{r@{:\;}r@{\;\redsem\;}ll}\mathsf{Com}&x!\langle a\rangle.P\;|\;x?(b).Q\;\to&P\;|\;Q[a/b]&\\
\mathsf{Bra}&x\triangleleft\left\{\ell:P_{\ell}\right\}_{\ell\in L}\;\to&x\triangleleft\left\{\ell_{k}:P_{\ell_{k}}\right\}&\mbox{if }\ell_{k}\in L\\
\mathsf{Sel}&x\triangleleft\left\{\ell:P_{\ell_{k}}\right\}\;|\;x\triangleright\left\{\ell:Q_{\ell}\right\}_{\ell\in L}\;\to&P_{\ell_{k}}\;|\;Q_{\ell_{k}}&\mbox{if }\ell_{k}\in L\end{array}&\begin{array}[]{r@{\;:\;}r@{\;\redsem\;}l@{\quad\mbox{if}\quad}l}\mathsf{Res}&(\nu x)P\;\to&(\nu x)P^{\prime}&P\to P^{\prime}\\
\mathsf{Par}&P\;|\;Q\;\to&P^{\prime}\;|\;Q&P\to P^{\prime}\\
\mathsf{Struc}&P\;\to&Q&P\equiv P^{\prime}\to Q^{\prime}\equiv Q\end{array}\end{array}\end{array}

Figure 2:

Syntax for processes, the relations generating the structural equivalence (
\equiv
), and the reduction semantics of the
\pi
-calculus.
The
\alpha
-equivalence is defined in the usual way (see Appendix).

We consider the version of
\pi
-calculus presented in
[
85
,
32
]
, whose processes are generated from a countable set of
(channel) names

\mathcal{N}=\{x,y,\ldots\}
and (disjoint) finite set of
labels

\mathcal{L}
grammar in
Figure

2
.

5
5

5

As standard, may write
x!\langle y\rangle
(resp.
x?(y)
) instead of
x!\langle y\rangle.\mathsf{Nil}
(resp.
x?(y).\mathsf{Nil}
).

In the same figure, we recall the definition of the
structural equivalence
(
\equiv
), as well as the
reduction semantics
.
We write
P\not\equiv Q
if
P\equiv Q
does not hold.
We may denote by
\mathcal{N}[P]
a process of the form
(\nu x_{1}){\cdots(\nu x_{n}){(P\;|\;Q)}}
for some names
x_{1},\ldots x_{n}
and a process
Q
, and write
a
instead of
a.\mathsf{Nil}
if
a\in\{x!\langle y\rangle,x?(y)\}
.
We denote by
\twoheadrightarrow
the transitive closure of
\to
.

A process
P
is
stuck
if
P\not\equiv\mathsf{Nil}
and there is no
P^{\prime}
such that

P\to P^{\prime}
.
A process P is called
deadlock-free
if
P
is not stuck and there is no stuck process
P^{\prime}
such that
P\twoheadrightarrow P^{\prime}
.
A process
P
is
race-free
if there is no
P^{\prime}
such that
P\twoheadrightarrow P^{\prime}
for a
P^{\prime}
structurally equivalent to one of the following processes:

\hfill\begin{array}[]{l@{\qquad\qquad}l}\mathcal{N}[(x!\langle y\rangle.R\;|\;x!\langle z\rangle.Q\;|\;S)]&\mathcal{N}[(x\triangleleft\left\{P_{\ell}\right\}_{\ell\in L}\;|\;x\triangleleft\left\{P_{\ell}\right\}_{\ell\in L^{\prime}}\;|\;S)]\\
\mathcal{N}[(x?(y).R\;|\;x?(z).Q\;|\;S)]&\mathcal{N}[(x\triangleright\left\{P_{\ell}\right\}_{\ell\in L}\;|\;x\triangleright\left\{P_{\ell}\right\}_{\ell\in L^{\prime}}\;|\;S)]\end{array}\hfill

(3)

A
execution trees
of a process
P
is a trees of processes with root
P
, where a process
Q^{\prime}
is a child of
Q
if
Q\to Q^{\prime}
, and such that branching is determined by the intrinsic non-determinism of the reduction rule
\mathsf{Bra}
, that is, if two processes
Q_{1}
and
Q_{2}
are children of a same process
Q
, then
Q\to Q_{1}
and
Q\to Q_{2}
via
\mathsf{Bra}
applied to the same minimal (w.r.t. term inclusion) sub-process of
Q
.
We may label the edges of a execution tree with the unique reduction rule in
\{\mathsf{Com},\mathsf{Bra},\mathsf{Sel}\}
required to reduce the term
P
to
Q
.
6
6

6

The reduction rules
\mathsf{Res}
,
\mathsf{Par}
and
\mathsf{Struc}
are not “meaningful” with respect to the computation, and even if a transition step may require multiple instances of these rules to deal with the bureaucracy of the syntax and the structural congruence, only a single instance of a rule in
\{\mathsf{Com},\mathsf{Bra},\mathsf{Sel}\}
is required to perform a reduction step.
For a formal definition of the labelling of the execution tree, see the definition of
core-reduction
in
[
8
]
.

The
interleaving
equivalence relation (
\sim
) on execution trees is defined by the relations in
Figure

3
.
See
Figure

4
for an example of two execution trees equivalent modulo interleaving.

3
A New Logical Framework for the
\pi
-calculus

\begin{array}[]{c|c|c}\mbox{Formulas}&\mbox{De Morgan Laws}&\mbox{$\alpha$-equivalence}\\
\begin{array}[]{l@{\;}c@{\;}llll}A,B&\coloneqq&\circ&\mbox{unit (atom)}\\

&\mid&(x\wn y)&\mbox{atom}\\
&\mid&A\invamp B&\mbox{par}\\
&\mid&A\mathop{\otimes}B&\mbox{tensor}\\
&\mid&A\blacktriangleleft B&\mbox{prec}\\
&\mid&A\mathop{\oplus}B&\mbox{oplus}\\
&\mid&A\with B&\mbox{with}\\
&\mid&\forall{x}.A&\mbox{for all}\\
&\mid&\exists{x}.A&\mbox{exists}\\
&\mid&\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.A&\mbox{new}\\
&\mid&\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}{x}.A&\mbox{ya}\end{array}&\begin{array}[]{ccc}{\circ}^{\bot}&=&\circ\\
{({A}^{\bot})}^{\bot}&=&A\\
{\langle x\oc y\rangle}^{\bot}&=&(x\wn y)\\
{(A\invamp B)}^{\bot}&=&{A}^{\bot}\mathop{\otimes}{B}^{\bot}\\
{(A\blacktriangleleft B)}^{\bot}&=&{A}^{\bot}\blacktriangleleft{B}^{\bot}\\
{(A\mathop{\oplus}B)}^{\bot}&=&{A}^{\bot}\with{B}^{\bot}\\
{(\forall x.A)}^{\bot}&=&\exists{x}.{A}^{\bot}\\
{(\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{\mathcal{X}}.A)}^{\bot}&=&\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}{\mathcal{X}}.{A}^{\bot}\end{array}&\begin{array}[]{c}a=a\\

\mbox{if $A_{i}=B_{i}$}\\
\mbox{and $\circleddot\in\{\invamp,\blacktriangleleft,\mathop{\otimes},\mathop{\oplus},\with\}$}\\
\\
\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}{x}.A=\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}{y}.A[y/x]\\
\mbox{$y$ fresh for $A$}\mbox{and $\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}\in\{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}{},\forall,\exists\}$}\end{array}\end{array}

Figure 5:
Formulas (with
x,y\in\mathcal{V}
), and their syntactic equivalences.

In this section we construct proof systems extending
first-order multiplicative additive linear logic
(or
\mathsf{MALL}^{1}
) with new operators allowing us to fitfully capture the behavior of term constructors for processes of the
\pi
-calculus w.r.t. the reduction semantics.

For this purpose, we enrich the language of
\mathsf{MALL}^{1}
with a non-commutative connective
\blacktriangleleft
designed to capture the logical properties of the (non-commutative) prefix operator used in the
\pi
-calculus
[
69
]
(but also in
CCS

[
68
]
).
Even if it would be desirable to require
\blacktriangleleft
to be associative, to capture the associativity of sequential composition of processes, we instead let
\blacktriangleleft
being non-associative to reflect the fact that the prefix operator only allows prefixing a single atomic action at a time, and thus it does not model sequential composition because unable to compose sequentially non-atomic processes.

To capture restriction, following the spirit of the nominal quantifiers as introduced in
[
30
]
, we use the nominal quantifier
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}
allowing variable binding.
As already explained in
[
67
]
, the universal quantifier cannot not be used to satisfactorily model restriction. For an example, consider the processes
Q=(\nu x)(\nu y)(\mathsf{Nil}!\langle x\rangle.a\;|\;\mathsf{Nil}?(y).a)
and
R=(\nu z)(\mathsf{Nil}!\langle z\rangle.a\;|\;\mathsf{Nil}?(z).a)
: if we encode restriction by universal quantification, then any property for
Q
should also be valid for
R
, because
\forall{x}.\forall{y}.P(x,y)
entails
\forall{z}.P(z,z)
.
The use of the existential quantifiers to model the variable binding of the input action, and nominal quantifiers for restriction allow us to avoid an unsound semantical overlap due to the duality of existential and universal quantification.
For example, if restriction were modelled by the universal quantifier, then the deadlocked process
(\nu a){x!\langle a\rangle.\mathsf{Nil}}\;|\;x?(a).\mathsf{Nil}
would be encoded by the tautology
(\forall{a}.(\langle x\oc a\rangle\blacktriangleleft\circ))\invamp(\exists{a}.((x\wn a)\blacktriangleleft\circ))=(\exists{a}.((x\wn a)\blacktriangleleft\circ))\multimap(\exists{a}.((x\wn a)\blacktriangleleft\circ))
, while
Theorem

47
shows that the formula encoding the process should not be provable. This mismatch is due to the translation, which allows unsound interactions between the binding of input actions with binding of restriction via a duality which is not valid in the semantics.

Remark 1
.

In our work, we do not consider a self-dual nominal quantifier as the one studied in
[
67
,
23
,
78
]
, but we rather introduce a dual quantifier similarly to what is done in
[
45
,
46
,
48
]
, where such a design choice is justified in view of the semantics of the
\pi
-calculus.

In
[
48
]
the authors list the three following logical properties a nominal quantifier
\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}
modeling the binder should satisfy:

1.

equivariance
,
\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}{x}.\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}{y}.A
and
\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}{y}.\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}{x}.A
should be logically equivalent;

2.

non-diagonality
: the formula
\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}{x}.\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}{y}.A(x,y)
should not imply
\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}{z}.A(z,z)
or vice versa;

3.

scope extrusion
:
if
\ominus
is a connective modeling parallelism, then

(\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}{x}.A)\ominus B
implies
\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}{x}.(A\ominus B)
whenever
x
does not occur in
B
.

In our work, all these requirements are met (see
Proposition

11
), but we also claim that the following additional condition should be added in this list, in view of how restriction and choice operators interact.

[4]

1.

name-choice
:
if
\circleddot
is a connective modeling choice, then
\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}{x}.A\circleddot\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}{x}.B
should imply
\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}{x}.\!\left(A\circleddot B\right)
.

Intuitively, this latter requirement is dictated by the observational indistinguishably of a process spawning a fresh name before making a global choice, and a process spawning a fresh name after such a choice is made.

Note that in
[
73
]
this latter condition is required to hold for all connectives, and in
[
48
]
such condition holds for the sequential operator.
However, such a behavior may not be desirable in certain contexts where two processes executed in sequence may behave differently if they share a communication channel or not.
For an example, consider the case in which a communication channel become loose or vulnerable to attacks after events depending on the use of the channel.

Definition 2
.

Formulas
are generated by a countable set of
variables
(
\mathcal{V}
) by the grammar in
Figure

5
modulo the standard

De Morgan Laws
and

\alpha
-equivalence

from the same figure.
A
context
is a formula containing a special occurrence of an atomic variable
\bullet
(called
hole
) and we denote by
\mathcal{C}[A]
the formula obtained by replacing
\bullet
with a formula
A
.
An
atom
is either the
unit

\circ
, or a predicate
\langle x\oc y\rangle
or
(x\wn y)
.
The
(linear) implication

A\multimap B
is defined as
{A}^{\bot}\invamp B
, where the
negation
is defined over formulas by extending the negation on atoms via the
de Morgan laws
in
Figure

5
.

For each formula, we define the set
\mathsf{free}(A)
of
free variables
as the set of variables occurring in
A
which are not bounded by any quantifier.
The free variables in a sequent
\Gamma=A_{1},\ldots,A_{n}
is the set
\mathsf{free}(\Gamma)=\bigcap_{i=1}^{n}\mathsf{free}(A_{i})
.
From now on, we assume sequents to be
clean
, that is, such that each variable
x
can occur bound by at most a universal quantifier, or by two dual nominal quantifiers.

Remark 3
.

To provide a lighter presentation of our systems, as well as to highlight the connections with the
\pi
-calculus, in this paper we consider formulas whose propositional atoms are generated by a limited signature containing no function symbols and two “dual” binary predicates
\langle-\oc-\rangle
and
(-\wn-)
.
However, a more expressive extension could be easily defined, and the results presented in this paper could be straightforwardly extended by addressing simple technical nuances, which we highlight in this paper whenever relevant.

Figure 6:

Sequent calculus rules with side conditions
\dagger\coloneqq x\notin\mathsf{free}(\Gamma)
.
The system
\mathsf{PiL}
is made of the rules above the double line. The rules below it are derivable.

Definition 4
.

A
nominal variable
is an element of the form
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x^{\nabla}}
with
x\in\mathcal{V}
and
\nabla\in\{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}\}
.
If
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}
is a set of nominal variables, we say that
x

occurs
in
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}
if
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x^{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}}}
or
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x^{\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}}}
is an element of
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}
.
A
(nominal) store

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}
is a set of nominal variables such that each variable occurs at most once in
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}
.
A
judgement

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma
consists of a store
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}
, and a clean sequent
\Gamma
.

Notation 5
.

We write judgements
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma
with

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}=\varnothing

(resp.
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}=\{{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x_{1}^{\nabla_{1}}},\ldots,{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x_{n}^{\nabla_{n}}}\}
)
simply as

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma
(resp.
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x_{1}^{\nabla_{1}}},\ldots,{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x_{n}^{\nabla_{n}}}}}\vdash\Gamma
, i.e., omitting parenthesis).
We write
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}_{1},{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}_{2}
to denote the (disjoint) union of two stores such that a same variable does not occur in both
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}_{1}
and
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}_{2}
.

We define rule systems using rules from
Figure

6
.
The rules in
Figure

6
in the first block are standard rules for the first-order multiplicative and additive fragment of linear logic decorated with stores.
As expected, rules
\mathop{\otimes}
and
\mathsf{mix}
split the context (and thus the store) among premises to enforce the linear use of resources, which is typical for multiplicative rules.
In contrast, the rule
\with
(with) duplicates the context (and thus the store).
The rules for the connective
\blacktriangleleft
in the second block are also multiplicative in this sense, as they maintain the same context-splitting behavior.
The rules
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\circ}
and
\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\circ}
simply remove quantification respecting the freshness condition (
\dagger
), as the standard rule
\forall
for the universal quantifier.
We are not making use of substitution for these rules because we assume
\alpha
-renaming could be applied to the formula prior to the application of the rule, in order to satisfy the side condition
\dagger
.
Similarly, the rule
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}}
(resp.
\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}}
) removes quantification respecting the freshness condition
\dagger
, as the standard rule
\forall
for the universal quantifier, but it also adds to the store the nominal variable
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x^{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}}}
(resp.
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x^{\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}}}
), where
x
is the variable bound by the nominal quantifier of the principal formula.
The rule
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{pop}}
(resp.
\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\mathsf{pop}}
) behaves similarly to the rule
\exists
for the existential quantifier, but removing an occurrence of the dual nominal quantifier
\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}
(resp.
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}
).
The name is due to the fact that the variable used for the substitution has to be a nominal variable
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x^{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}}}
(resp.
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x^{\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}}}
) in the store.

We prove in this section the admissibility of the that the rules below the double line, which are the standard rules for the general (non-atomic) axiom and cut, and a special rule
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}\mathchar 45\relax\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}
removing a pair of dual nominal quantifiers binding the same variable
x
.

Definition 6
.

We define the following systems using rules from
Figure

6
.

\begin{array}[]{r@{\;=\;}l@{\quad}r@{\;=\;}l@{\quad}r@{\;=\;}l}\mathsf{MLL}&\left\{\mathsf{ax},\invamp,\mathop{\otimes}\right\}&\mathsf{MLL}^{\circ}&\mathsf{MLL}\cup\{\circ,\mathsf{mix}\}\\
\mathsf{MALL}&\mathsf{MLL}\cup\left\{\mathop{\oplus},\with\right\}&\mathsf{MALL}_{1}&\mathsf{MALL}\cup\left\{\forall,\exists\right\}\\
\mathsf{NML}&\mathsf{MLL}\cup\left\{\blacktriangleleft,\blacktriangleleft_{\circ},\circ,\mathsf{mix}\right\}&\mathsf{NMAL}&\mathsf{MALL}\cup\left\{\blacktriangleleft,\blacktriangleleft_{\circ},\circ,\mathsf{mix}\right\}\\
\mathsf{mini}\mathchar 45\relax\mathsf{PiL}&\mathsf{NMAL}\cup\left\{\exists,\forall,\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\circ},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\circ},\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}\mathchar 45\relax\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}\right\}&\mathsf{PiL}^{-}&\mathsf{NMAL}\cup\left\{\exists,\forall,\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\circ},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\circ},\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}},\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{pop}}\right\}\\
\lx@intercol\hfil\mathsf{PiL}=\mathsf{MALL}_{1}\cup\left\{\blacktriangleleft,\blacktriangleleft_{\circ},\circ,\mathsf{mix}\right\}\cup\left\{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\circ},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\circ},\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}},\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{pop}},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\mathsf{pop}}\right\}\hfil\lx@intercol\end{array}

(4)

If
\mathsf{X}
is a system, we write
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{X}}\,}\Gamma
to denote that
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\varnothing}\vdash\Gamma
is derivable in
\mathsf{X}
.

Remark 7
.

During proof search, the nominal quantifier
\nabla\in\{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}\}
could be removed by a rule
\nabla_{\mathsf{load}}
, storing the variable bound by the nominal quantifier in the store (as a nominal variable).
Since the axiom rule and the unit rule have empty store, each nominal variable
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x^{\nabla}}
in the store must be used for the substitution of a variable bound by the dual nominal quantifier
{\nabla}^{\bot}
.
That is, any derivation establishes some pairing between each
\nabla_{\mathsf{load}}
with some
\nabla_{\mathsf{pop}}
rules above it in a derivation – in absence of additive connectives, such a
\nabla_{\mathsf{pop}}
above the
\nabla_{\mathsf{load}}
is unique.

A similar pairing can be observed in the weaker rule
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}\mathchar 45\relax\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}
, which removes a pair of dual nominal quantifiers binding the same variable
x
.
However, such a localized interaction rules out the possibility to prove quantifier swaps for nominal quantifiers and the nominal-choice laws from
Equation

5
.

Remark 8
.

The pair
\langle\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}\rangle
of nominal quantifiers in
\mathsf{PiL}
behaves differently from the pair
\langle\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}},\mathord{\text{\char 221\relax}}\rangle
considered by Horne and Tiu for the logic
\mathsf{BV}^{1}
and its extensions
[
45
,
46
,
48
]
.
One difference is the way
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}
and
\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}
interact in
\mathsf{PiL}
, in which each nominal quantifier
\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}
interacts with at most one dual quantifier
{\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}}^{\bot}
,
while in
\mathsf{BV}^{1}
a
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}
can interact with multiple
\mathord{\text{\char 221\relax}}
.
By means of example, the implication
(\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.A\mathop{\otimes}\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.B)\multimap\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.\!\left(A\invamp B\right)
(i.e., the formula
\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}{x}.{A}^{\bot}\invamp\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}{x}.{B}^{\bot}\invamp\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.\!\left(A\invamp B\right)
) is provable in
\mathsf{BV}^{1}
but not in
\mathsf{PiL}
.

This reminds the different ways the modalities in the modal logics
\mathsf{M}
and
\mathsf{K}
interacts via the rules:
in the former, each diamond (
\Diamond
)interacts with exectly one box (
\Box
), while in the latter, multiple diamonds can interact with a single box, as shown in the sequent rules of their sequent calculi – see
[
57
,
59
,
11
]
for additional details.

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash B,A

\scriptstyle\mathsf{M}\;

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Diamond B,\Box A

and

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash B_{1},\ldots,B_{n},A

\scriptstyle\mathsf{K}\;

n\in\mathbb{N}

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Diamond B_{1},\ldots,\Diamond B_{n},\Box A

Moreover, the implication
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.A\multimap{\left(\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.{A}^{\bot}\right)}^{\bot}
(that is, the formula
\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}{x}.A\invamp\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}{x}.A
) is not derivable in
\mathsf{PiL}
, while it is in
\mathsf{BV}^{1}
.

Another difference depends on the way nominal quantifiers interact with the connective modeling sequentiality.
Our nominal quantifiers do not satisfy scope extrusion over sequentiality, that is, the formula
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.(A\blacktriangleleft B)\multimapboth(\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.A)\blacktriangleleft B
with
x\notin\mathsf{free}(B)
is not derivable in
\mathsf{PiL}
.
However, this property is striclty needed in
\mathsf{BV}^{1}
in order to guarantee that the logical implication is a transitive relation (i.e., that if
A\multimap B
and
B\multimap C
are derivable, then also
A\multimap C
is derivable).

4
Proof theoretical properties of
\mathsf{PiL}

In this section we prove the proof theoretical properties of the system
\mathsf{PiL}
, including the derivability of rules and the possibility of embedding
\mathsf{PiL}
in
\mathsf{MAV}^{1}
.

Our systems satisfy the property referred to as
initial coherence

[
15
,
66
]
, that is, the property that atomic axioms suffice to guarantee the possibility of deriving the general axiom rule.
Said differently, in
\mathsf{PiL}
we can derive any formula of the form
A\multimap A
using axiom rules restricted on atoms only.

Proposition 9
.

Then the rule
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}\mathchar 45\relax\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}
is derivable in
\{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}},\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{pop}}\}
.

Proof.

It suffices to remark that each instance of
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}\mathchar 45\relax\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}
can be replaced by a
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}}
followed (bottom-up) by a
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{pop}}
.
∎

Proposition 10
.

Then the rule
\mathsf{AX}
is derivable in
\mathsf{MALL}^{1}\cup\{\circ,\blacktriangleleft,\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}},\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{pop}}\}
.

Proof.

We that the judgement
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash{A}^{\bot},A
is derivable in
\mathsf{MALL}^{1}\cup\{\circ,\blacktriangleleft,\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}\mathchar 45\relax\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}\}
for any formula
A
by induction on the structure of
A
:

•

if
A=\circ
, then such a derivation is made of a
\mathsf{mix}
with premises of the form
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\circ
, each conclusion of a
\circ
-rule;

•

if
A=B\blacktriangleleft C
, then
{A}^{\bot}={B}^{\bot}\blacktriangleleft{C}^{\bot}
.
We apply a rule
\blacktriangleleft
, and we conclude by inductive hypothesis;

•

if
A=\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}{x}.B
with
\nabla\in\{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}\}
, then we apply (bottom-up) a rule
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}\mathchar 45\relax\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}
-rule and we conclude by inductive hypothesis;

•

otherwise, we proceed as standard in
\mathsf{MALL}_{1}
.

The statement follow from
Proposition

9
.
∎

We have the following properties for our connectives, quantifiers and unit. Note that the list in
Equation

5
is not complete, since additional implications and equivalences immediately follow by duality.

Proposition 11
.

The following logical equivalences and implications are derivable in
\mathsf{PiL}
.

\begin{array}[]{c}\begin{array}[]{c|c}\mbox{Unit Laws}&\mbox{Monoidal Laws}\\
\begin{array}[]{r@{\feq}c@{\feq}l}(A\invamp\circ)\multimapboth&(A\mathop{\otimes}\circ)\hfil\multimapboth&A\\
(A\blacktriangleleft\circ)\multimapboth&(\circ\blacktriangleleft A)\hfil\multimapboth&A\\
(\circ\with\circ)\multimapboth&(\circ\mathop{\oplus}\circ)\hfil\multimapboth&\circ\end{array}&\begin{array}[]{c}A\circleddot B\multimapboth B\circleddot A\\
(A\circleddot B)\circleddot C\multimapboth A\circleddot(B\circleddot C)\\
\mbox{with }\circleddot\in\{\invamp,\mathop{\otimes},\mathop{\oplus},\with\}\end{array}\\
\forall{x}.\circ\multimapboth\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.\circ\multimapboth\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}{x}.\circ\multimapboth\exists{x}.\circ\multimapboth\circ\\
\hline\cr\mbox{Scope extrusion}&\mbox{Quantifier Swap}\\
\begin{array}[]{c}\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.(A\invamp B)\multimapboth(\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.A)\invamp B\\
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.B\multimapboth B\\
\mbox{if $x\notin\mathsf{free}(B)$}\end{array}&\begin{array}[]{r@{\feq}l}\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}{x}.\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}{y}.A\multimapboth&\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}{y}.\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}{x}.A\\
\lx@intercol\hfil\mbox{with }\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}\in\{\exists,\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}},\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}},\forall\}\hfil\lx@intercol\end{array}\\
\hline\cr\mbox{Multiplicative refinement}&\mbox{Quantifier refinement}\\
\begin{array}[]{c@{\limp}c}(A\mathop{\otimes}B)\hfil\multimap&(A\blacktriangleleft B)\\
(A\blacktriangleleft B)\hfil\multimap&(A\invamp B)\end{array}&\begin{array}[]{c@{\qquad}c}\forall{x}.A\multimap\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.A&\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.A\multimap\exists{x}.A\\
\forall{x}.A\multimap\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}{x}.A&\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}{x}.A\multimap\exists{x}.A\end{array}\\
\hline\cr\mbox{Nominal-choice}&\mbox{Distributivity of choice}\\
\begin{array}[]{c@{\;}c@{\;}c}(\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.A\with\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.B)&\multimapboth&(\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.(A\with B))\\
(\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.A\oplus\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.B)&\multimapboth&(\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.(A\oplus B))\end{array}&\begin{array}[]{c}((A\invamp B)\with(A\invamp C))\multimap(A\invamp(B\with C))\\
(A\invamp(B\with C))\multimap((A\invamp B)\with(A\invamp C))\\
(A\invamp(B\mathop{\oplus}C))\multimap((A\mathop{\oplus}B)\invamp(A\mathop{\oplus}C))\end{array}\end{array}\end{array}

Monodail laws are proven as standard in
\mathsf{MALL}
.
Scope extrusion and nominal quantifiers swaps are proven as shown in
Equation

6
below.

\scriptstyle\mathsf{AX}\;

\vdash{A}^{\bot},A

\scriptstyle\mathsf{AX}\;

\vdash{B}^{\bot},B

\scriptstyle\mathop{\otimes}\;

\vdash({A}^{\bot}\mathop{\otimes}{B}^{\bot}),A,B

\scriptstyle\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{pop}}\;

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x^{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}}}}\vdash\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}{x}.({A}^{\bot}\mathop{\otimes}{B}^{\bot}),A,B

\scriptstyle\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}}\;

\vdash\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}{x}.({A}^{\bot}\mathop{\otimes}{B}^{\bot}),\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.A,B

\scriptstyle 2\times\invamp\;

\vdash\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}{x}.({A}^{\bot}\mathop{\otimes}{B}^{\bot})\invamp((\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.A)\invamp B)

\scriptstyle\mathsf{AX}\;

\vdash{A}^{\bot},A

\scriptstyle 2\times\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{pop}}\;

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x^{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}y^{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}}}}\vdash\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}{y}.\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}{x}.{A}^{\bot}

\scriptstyle 2\times\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}}\;

\vdash\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{y}.A\invamp\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}{y}.\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}{x}.{A}^{\bot}

(6)

Quantifier swap for universal and existential quantifiers are standard as in in
\mathsf{MALL}_{1}
.
For multiplicative refinement we only show the derivation for
(A\mathop{\otimes}B)\multimap(A\blacktriangleleft B)
on the left of
Equation

7
, since the derivation for
(A\blacktriangleleft B)\multimap(A\invamp B)
is similar.
Nominal refinements are proven as shown in the right of
Equation

7
below.

\scriptstyle\mathsf{AX}\;

\vdash A,{A}^{\bot}

\scriptstyle\mathsf{AX}\;

\vdash B,{B}^{\bot}

\scriptstyle\blacktriangleleft_{\circ}\;

\vdash{A}^{\bot},{B}^{\bot},A\blacktriangleleft B

\scriptstyle\invamp\;

\vdash{A}^{\bot}\invamp{B}^{\bot},A\blacktriangleleft B

\scriptstyle\invamp\;

\vdash({A}^{\bot}\invamp{B}^{\bot})\invamp(A\blacktriangleleft B)

\scriptstyle\mathsf{AX}\;

\vdash{A}^{\bot},A

\scriptstyle\exists\;

\vdash\exists{x}.{A}^{\bot},A

\scriptstyle\nabla_{\circ}\;

\vdash\exists{x}.{A}^{\bot},\nabla x.A

\scriptstyle\invamp\;

\vdash\exists{x}.{A}^{\bot}\invamp\nabla x.A

(7)

Finally, distributivity of the choice are standard in
\mathsf{MALL}
(they are proven by applying (bottom-up)
\invamp
and
\with
rules first, followed by
\mathop{\oplus}
and
\mathop{\otimes}
rules.), and nominal-choice laws are proven as follows.

Remark 12
.

The system
\mathsf{mini}\mathchar 45\relax\mathsf{PiL}
satisfies all the equivalences and implications in
Proposition

11
, except for quantifier swap and nominal choices,
while the system
\mathsf{PiL}^{-}
satisfies all the equivalences and implications in
Proposition

11
, except for the bottom-most nominal choice.
For this latter, it only satisfies the left-to-right implication
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{PiL}^{-}}\,}(\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.A\oplus\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.B)\multimap(\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.(A\oplus B))
(see the right branch of the bottom-most derivation in
Equation

8
), but not the converse.

Figure 8:
Cut-elimination steps for the connective
\blacktriangleleft
and its rules.

We prove the admissibility of the rule
\mathsf{cut}
, we provide a cut-elimination procedure adapting the one for
\mathsf{MALL}_{1}
.
In absence of the nominal quantifier, the proof taking into account the connective
\blacktriangleleft
is straightforward.
In the presence of the nominal quantifier, the proof is more intricate because of the implicit links between
\nabla_{\mathsf{load}}
-rules and
\nabla_{\mathsf{pop}}
-rules in a derivation we discuss in
Remark

7
.
For example, consider the derivation with
\mathsf{cut}
of the formula
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.a\multimap\nabla x.a
in the left of
Equation

9
, where we marked the flows of the nominal variables.

(9)

In order to perform cut-elimination, we need to be able to keeping track of the variables bound by dual nominal quantifiers, which are supposed to be linked by the
\mathsf{cut}
-rule, even when the nominal quantifiers are removed.
For this purpose, we introduce the following auxiliary
store-cut
rule we use during the rewriting process of cut-elimination.

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x^{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x^{\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}}}}\vdash\Gamma

\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}\mathchar 45\relax\mathsf{cut}\;

{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma

(10)

Theorem 13

(Cut elimination)
.

Let
\Gamma
a non-empty sequent.
If
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{PiL}\cup\{\mathsf{cut}\}}\,}\Gamma
, then
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{PiL}}\,}\Gamma
.

Proof.

We define the
weight
of a
\mathsf{cut}
-rule
{\mathsf{r}}
in a derivation
\mathcal{D}
as a pair
\langle\mathsf{d}_{\mathcal{D}}\left({\mathsf{r}}\right),\mathsf{c}_{\mathcal{D}}\left({\mathsf{r}}\right)\rangle
where
\mathsf{d}_{\mathcal{D}}\left({\mathsf{r}}\right)
is the maximal distance of
{\mathsf{r}}
from a leaf above it in the derivation tree,
and
\mathsf{c}_{\mathcal{D}}\left({\mathsf{r}}\right)
is the complexity of the active formula(s) of
{\mathsf{r}}
.
The
weight
of a
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}\mathchar 45\relax\mathsf{cut}
-rule
{\mathsf{r}}
is defined similarly as
\langle\mathsf{d}_{\mathcal{D}}\left({\mathsf{r}}\right),0\rangle
.
The
weight
of a derivation is the multiset of the weights of its
\mathsf{cut}
-rules and
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}\mathchar 45\relax\mathsf{cut}
-rules.

To prove cut-elimination it suffices to apply the
cut-elimination steps
in
Figures

7
,
8
and
9
to a top-most
\mathsf{cut}
-rule or
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}\mathchar 45\relax\mathsf{cut}
-rule in the derivation tree.
The fact that we consider the procedure to operate on a derivation whose conclusion and premises judgements have empty stores and non-empty sequents ensures that the case analysis we consider covers all the possible cases.
In particular, the case
\circ\mbox{-vs-}\circ
in
Figure

7
for the
\circ
(because the sequent in the conclusion cannot be empty), and the bottom-most case in
Figure

9
(because the store in the conclusion and in the premises is empty).

In order to be able to apply this strategy, as standard in the literature, we consider the
commutative cut-elimination steps
, that is, rule permutations as the ones in
Figure

16
involving a
\mathsf{cut}
-rule or a
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}\mathchar 45\relax\mathsf{cut}
-rule, allowing us to permute an instance of such rule above another rules.
The termination of cut-elimination follows by the fact that each cut-elimination step applied to a top-most
\mathsf{cut}
-rule
{\mathsf{r}}
decreases
\mathsf{c}_{\mathcal{D}}\left({\mathsf{r}}\right)
, while each commutative cut-elimination step applied to the top-most
\mathsf{cut}
-rule, or to a
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}\mathchar 45\relax\mathsf{cut}
-rule reduces
\mathsf{d}_{\mathcal{D}}\left({\mathsf{r}}\right)
.
Note that a commutative step moving a
\mathsf{cut}
-rule above a
\with
-rule duplicate the
\mathsf{cut}
-rule.
This is why we have to define the weight as a multiset: even if the complexity does not change, the maximal distance from these two new
\mathsf{cut}
-rules from the leaves is strictly smaller than the one of the original one.
∎

Remark 14
.

In systems containing a self-dual unit
\circ
, which is the same unit for conjunction and disjunction, such as multiplicative linear logic with mix
[
33
]
,
\mathsf{Pomset}
logic
[
75
]
and
\mathsf{BV}

[
40
]
, it is possible to derive the empty sequent.
This depends on the fact the empty sequent is not interpreted as false (as in classical logic), but rather as the unit
\circ
, which is provable, and that the non-admissibility of the weakening rule (as in relevant logics
[
12
,
10
]
) would not entail the possibility of deriving any sequent.
Citing Girard (as reported in
[
18
]
) “if one were to accept this rule [
\mathsf{mix}
], the good taste would require to add the void sequent as an axiom (without weakening this has no dramatic consequence)”.
This explains the structure of the cut-elimination step
\circ
-vs-
\circ
in
Figure

7
.

Remark 15
.

If we consider a system where the only rule for nominal quantifier is the rule
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}\mathchar 45\relax\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}
, then all judgements in derivations have empty store.

Note that the system
\mathsf{PiL}\setminus\{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{pop}},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}}\}
presented in
[
60
]
also satisfy cut-elimination, and it already expressive enought to support the interpreting derivations as execution trees (see
Section

7
).
Indeed, the only difference is that in such a system the nominal-choice law
(\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.A\oplus\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.B)\multimapboth(\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.(A\oplus B))
does not hold, but only the left-to-right implication is provable as explained in
Remark

12
.

Corollary 16
.

The linear implication (
\multimap
) in
\mathsf{PiL}
defines a transitive relation, that is, if
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{PiL}}\,}A\multimap B
and
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{PiL}}\,}B\multimap C
, then
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{PiL}}\,}A\multimap C
.

Proof.

If
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{PiL}}\,}A\multimap B
, then there is a derivation
\mathcal{D}^{-}_{A\multimap B}
with conclusion
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash{A}^{\bot},B
because the rule
\invamp
is invertible (that is, its conclusion is derivable iff its premise is so).
For the same reason, by hypothesis, there is a derivation
\mathcal{D}^{-}_{B\multimap C}
in
\mathsf{PiL}
with conclusion
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash{B}^{\bot},C
.
Thus a derivation with conclusion
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash A\multimap C
made of (bottom-up) a
\invamp
-rule followed by a
\mathsf{cut}
-rule whose premises are the conclusion of
\mathcal{D}^{-}_{A\multimap B}
and
\mathcal{D}^{-}_{B\multimap C}
.
We conclude by applying cut-elimination.
∎

We conclude this section stating that
\mathsf{PiL}
can be embedded in
\mathsf{MAV}^{1}

[
48
]
using a translation
\left\lceil\cdot\right\rceil
replacing each occurrence of
\blacktriangleleft
with a
\triangleleft
, and each occurrence of
\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}
with a
\mathord{\text{\char 221\relax}}
.
Formal definitions and details of the proof are provided in
Appendix

A
.

Theorem 17
.

Let
A_{1},\ldots,A_{n}
be formulas.
If
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{PiL}}\,}A_{1},\ldots,A_{n}
, then
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{MAV}^{1}}\,}{}_{i=1}^{n}\left\lceil A_{i}\right\rceil
.

5
Proof Nets for
\mathsf{PiL}

In this section, we define proof nets for
\mathsf{PiL}
and we prove soundness and completeness of this syntax by providing sequentialization and proof translation (desequentialization) procedures.

To handle the interaction between multiplicative (
\invamp
,
\mathop{\otimes}
and
\blacktriangleleft
) and additive (
\mathop{\oplus}
and
\with
) connectives in
\mathsf{PiL}
in a canonical way, we develop two syntaxes for proof nets:

•

conflict nets
(extending
[
53
,
52
]
):
these proof nets provide canonical representative for proofs modulo local rule permutations, with polynomial-time correctness criterion, sequentialization, and proof translation; and

•

slice nets

[
56
]
(extending
[
55
,
56
]
):
these proof nets provide canonical representative for proofs modulo rule permutations (inlcuding non-local ones), with polynomial-time correcness criterion and sequentialization, but no polynomial time proof translation.

In particular, the former syntax is optimal for the application we aim at in this paper (see
Section

6
).

In the reminder of this section, we first provide some shared definitions on links and dualizers.
We then define conflict nets, proving soundness and completeness by providing procedures for sequentialization and proof translation.
We then define slice nets and we prove soundness and completeness using the results on conflict nets.

We first adapt the definitions of links to take into account stores.

Definition 18
.

A
link

{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}
on a judgement
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma
(or a sequent
\Gamma
) is either

•

a
sub-judgement
of
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma
, that is, a judgement
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}}\vdash\Gamma^{\prime}
such that
\Gamma^{\prime}
is an induced sub-forest of
\Gamma
and
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}\subseteq S
; or

•

nominal link
: a pair
\{x,y\}
of variables occurring in
\Gamma
with
x
bound by
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}
and
y
by a
\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}
, or a pair of the form
\{{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x^{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}}},y\}
(resp.
\{{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x^{\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}}},y\}
) made of a nominal variable
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x^{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}}}
(resp.
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}x^{\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}}}
) in the store, and a variable
y
occurring in
\Gamma
bound by the nominal quantifier
\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}
(resp.
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}
);

A link is
axiomatic
if it is nominal link containing no nominal variables, or a sub-sequent made of a single occurrence of
\circ
or a pair of the atoms of the form
\{\langle x\oc y\rangle,(z\wn t)\}
.
A
linking
(resp.
axiomatic linking
) on
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma
is a set of links (resp. axiomatic links) on
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma
.

Notation 19
.

We represent a link
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}
by drawing a horizontal line labeled by
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}
connected via vertical segments to the roots of each variable or subformula in the link.

(11)

The sequent
\Gamma^{\prime}=D,D\oplus E
is not a link for the given judgement because it is not a sub-judgement since the formula
D
is repeated twice.

We then fix a notation for substitutions which we use to encode the information about the witnesses of the quantifiers.

Notation 21
.

We use the standard notation
\sigma=[x_{1}/y_{1},\ldots,x_{n}/y_{n}]
for
substitutions
, i.e., (partial) maps over the set of variables
7
7

7

In the language of
\mathsf{PiL}
we have no function symbols, but this definition could be generalized by defining a substitution as a map from variables to terms, as done in
[
42
]
.
with
domain

\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}\}
.
Moreover, we use the following denotations:

•

\delta_{\varnothing}
is the
empty substitution
;

•

\sigma\tau
is the
composition
of
\sigma
and
\tau
(in which
\sigma
is applied after
\tau
);

•

\sigma\setminus\{x\}
is the substitution obtained from
\tau

by removing the substitution of the variable
x
;

•

\sigma
is
more general
than
\tau

(denoted
\sigma\leq\rho
)
if there is a map
\rho
such that
\sigma\rho=\tau
;

•

\sigma
and
\tau
are
disjoint

(denoted
\mathsf{dis}(\sigma,\tau)
)
if so are their domains.
We may write

\sigma+\tau
to denote
\sigma\tau=\tau\sigma
whenever
\mathsf{dis}(\sigma,\tau)
;

•

\sigma
and
\tau
are
coherent

(denoted
\mathsf{coh}(\sigma,\tau)
)
if there is
\rho
such that
\sigma\rho=\tau\rho
;

•

the
join
of
\sigma
and
\tau
(denoted
\sigma\vee\tau
) is the least map
\rho
such that
\sigma\leq\rho
and
\tau\leq\rho
;

Definition 22
.

A
dualizer

\delta_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}
for a link
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}
on a judgement
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma
(or a sequent
\Gamma
) is a substitution with domain variables either occurring in
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}
, or occurring bound by an existential quantifier (
\exists
) or by a nominal quantifier (
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}
or
\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}
) in
\Gamma
.

A
linking with witnesses

\langle\Lambda,\delta^{\Lambda}\rangle
is a linking
\Lambda
on
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma
provided with a
witness map

\delta^{\Lambda}
associating to each link in
\Lambda
a (possibly empty) dualizer.

The
initial witness map
of an axiomatic linking
\Lambda
is defined as follows for each
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}\in\Lambda
:

•

if
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}=\{\langle x\oc y\rangle,(z\wn t)\}
, then
\delta_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}^{\Lambda}=[x/z,y/t]
;

•

if
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}=\{x,y\}
is a nominal link with
x
bound by
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}
and
y
bound by
\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}
, then
\delta_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}^{\Lambda}=[x]y
;

•

if
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}=\{\circ\}
, then
\delta_{\varnothing}
.

Figure 10:

Coalescence steps for co-trees, with
\nabla\in\{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}\}
and

leaves.

5.1
Conflict Nets

Conflict nets for
\mathsf{MALL}
are trees alternating
concord
(
\frown
) and
conflict
(
\#
) nodes, having the elements of an axiomatic linking as leaves, and satisfying a contractibility criterion with respect to a rewriting procedure called
coalescence
.

Definition 23
.

A
concord-conflict tree
(or
co-tree
for short) for a linking
\Lambda
on a judgement
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma
is a tree
\tau(\Lambda)
with leaves labeled by links
\Lambda
, and internal nodes labeled by
\frown
(
concord
nodes) or by
\#
(
conflict
nodes).
It is
axiomatic
if
\Lambda
is axiomatic.
We denote by
\left\lfloor\tau(\Lambda)\right\rfloor
the co-tree obtained by merging adjacent
\frown
-nodes (resp.
\#
-nodes), and by removing nodes with a single child (by attaching its child to its parent).
A co-tree
\tau(\Lambda)
is
canonical
if
\tau(\Lambda)=\left\lfloor\tau(\Lambda)\right\rfloor
.
We may denote
\tau(\Lambda)_{1}\frown\tau(\Lambda)_{2}
or
\frown\left(\tau(\Lambda)_{1},\ldots,\tau(\Lambda)_{n}\right)

(resp.
\tau(\Lambda)_{1}\#\tau(\Lambda)_{2}
or
\#\left(\tau(\Lambda)_{1},\ldots,\tau(\Lambda)_{n}\right)
)
a co-tree with root a
\frown
-node (resp.
\#
-node) having as children the roots of
\tau(\Lambda)_{1},\ldots,\tau(\Lambda)_{n}
.

As for linkings with witnesses, we define a
co-tree with witnesses

\langle\tau(\Lambda),\delta\rangle
as a co-tree
\tau(\Lambda)
equipped with a
witness map

\delta
associating to each leaf
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}
of
\tau(\Lambda)
a (possibly empty) dualizer
\delta_{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}}
.

In order to define the coalescence criterion, we need to consider co-trees for linkings with witnesses, rather than co-trees for linkings.

Definition 24
.

In
Figure

10
we define
coalescence steps
over co-trees with witnesses.
A co-tree
\tau(\Lambda)
for a linking
\Lambda
on
\vdash\Gamma
is
coalescent
if there is a
coalescence path
, that is, a sequence of coalescence steps from the co-tree with witnesses
\langle\tau(\Lambda),\delta^{\Lambda}\rangle
(where
\delta^{\tau(\Lambda)}
is the initial witness map for
\Lambda
) to a co-tree with witnesses consisting of a single leaf
\vdash\Gamma
with empty dualizer.

A
conflict net
for a sequent
\Gamma
is a coalescent axiomatic co-tree
\tau(\Lambda)
on
\vdash\Gamma
.

Theorem 25
.

Let
\Gamma
be a sequent.
Then
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{PiL}}\,}\Gamma
iff there is a conflict-net
\tau(\Lambda)
on
\Gamma
.

Proof.

For each derivation
\mathcal{D}
of
\Gamma
, we define the (axiomatic) co-tree
\left\{\!\left\{\mathcal{D}\right\}\!\right\}_{\mathsf{co}}
by translating top-down rules
\mathcal{D}
as shown in
Figure

11
.
Prove that
\tau(\Lambda)_{\mathcal{D}}
is coalescent is trivial: it suffices to consider a coalescence path where coalescence steps, which are in correspondence with rules in
\mathsf{PiL}
, respect the order in which we translate the proof – Note that rules
\mathsf{mix}
and
\blacktriangleleft_{\circ}
may require to be postponed during such translation, and applied out-of-order because of the side conditions we have on coalescence steps.

To prove the converse, we define
deductive co-trees
as co-trees with witnesses such that the leaves which are judgements are labeled by derivations with conclusion the corresponding judgement.
For the base case, we consider the initial axiomatic co-tree
\tau(\Lambda)
with witnesses
\delta^{\tau(\Lambda)}
whose leaves which are judgements are labeled by rules
\mathsf{ax}
or
\circ
.
We then define a derivation
\mathcal{D}_{\tau(\Lambda)}
with conclusion
\vdash\Gamma
as shown in
Figure

12
, reasoning by induction on the length of a given coalescence path for
\tau(\Lambda)
, which exists by definition of conflict net.
∎

Corollary 26

(Conflict nets for
\mathsf{MALL}^{1}
)
.

A sequent
\Gamma
is derivable in
\mathsf{MALL}^{1}
if it admits a coalescent slice net
\tau(\Lambda)
whose coalescence path only containing steps
\invamp
,
\mathop{\oplus}
,
\exists
,
\forall
,
\mathop{\otimes}
,
\with
,
\#
, and
\bullet
.

on co-trees with leaves labeled by derivations.
The steps

As in
[
52
]
, we define the
size
of a proof net
\tau(\Lambda)
on
\Gamma
as the number
|\tau(\Lambda)|
of nodes in the co-tree
\tau(\Lambda)
plus the number
|\Gamma|
of nodes in the forest
\Gamma
.

Proposition 27
.

The coalescence criterion is polynomial in the size of the proof net.

Proof.

The result follows from the same argument (and algorithms) used in
[
52
]
in the proof of the similar result for
\mathsf{MALL}
.
The new multiplicative coalescence steps (the ones involving the
\blacktriangleleft
) are as complex as the
\mathop{\otimes}
.
Coalescence steps involving quantifiers require to perform operations on dualizers which are linear in the size of the dualizer (see
[
61
]
), and the size of the dualizer is linear in the size of the formula.
Thus the complexity is at most
\mathcal{O}(n^{5})
where
n
is the size of the proof net.
∎

5.2
Slice Nets

In this paper we define slice nets using the correctness criterion from
[
53
]
based on
erasing steps
rather than on slicing and switchings as in
[
56
,
55
]
.
The criterion presented here is more similar to the criterion we used for conflict nets, it requires fewer definitions to be stated, and it is polynomial on the size of of a slice net.

Definition 28
.

The
parse graph
8
8

8

Indeed, parse graphs are always forests.
of a judgement
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma
is defined as the graph
\mathcal{G}\left({\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}\vdash\Gamma\right)
with:

•

set of vertices
\mathsf{V}({\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma)
contains the store
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}
, and the set of occurrences of atoms, connectives, quantifiers, and bound variables in the sequent
\Gamma
; and

•

set of edges
\mathsf{E}({\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma)
containing an edge
\{v,w\}
whenever
v
is the main operator of a formula
A=A_{1}\circleddot A_{2}
(resp.
A=\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}{x}.A_{1}
) and
w
is the main operator of the
A_{1}
or
A_{2}
(resp. of the subformula
A_{1}
or the variable
x
).

The parse graph of a sequent
\Gamma
or a formula
A
is defined similarly.

If
\Lambda\!\!\!\Lambda
is a set of axiomatic linkings on
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma
, then the
linked parse graph
is the graph
\mathcal{G}\left({\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}\vdash\Gamma::\Lambda\!\!\!\Lambda\right)
obtained by adding to
\mathcal{G}\left({\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}\vdash\Gamma\right)
the set of edges
\mathsf{E}(\Lambda\!\!\!\Lambda)
containing an edge between each pair of vertices corresponding to a pair of atoms or variables in link in one of the linking in
\Lambda\!\!\!\Lambda
– therefore, no edge has to be considered for a link of the form
\{\circ\}
.

Notation 29
.

Let
\Lambda\!\!\!\Lambda=\{\Lambda_{i}\}_{i\in I}
be a set of atomic linkings for a judgement
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma
.
If
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}}\vdash\Gamma^{\prime}
is a sub-judgement of
{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}}\vdash\Gamma
, then we define
\Lambda\!\!\!\Lambda|_{{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}}\vdash\Gamma^{\prime}}
as the set of non-empty linkings
\{\Lambda^{\prime}_{i}\}_{j\in J}
(for a
J\subseteq I
) such that each linking
\Lambda_{i}^{\prime}
contains all links in
\Lambda_{i}
which are pairs of vertices in
\mathsf{V}({\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}}\vdash\Gamma^{\prime})
,
that is,

\Lambda\!\!\!\Lambda|_{{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}}\vdash\Gamma^{\prime}}=\begin{Bmatrix}\Lambda_{i}|_{{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}}\vdash\Gamma^{\prime}}\coloneqq\{\lambda\in\Lambda_{i}\mid\lambda\subseteq\mathsf{V}({\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}}\vdash\Gamma^{\prime})\}\mid i\in I,\;\Lambda_{i}|_{{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}}\vdash\Gamma^{\prime}}\neq\varnothing\end{Bmatrix}
.

Definition 30
.

In
Figure

13
we define
erasing steps
as the rewriting rules over sets of linkings with witnesses
9
9

9

We represent erasing steps without explicitly writing the context, that is, if
L\rightarrow_{\mathsf{er}}R_{1},\ldots,R_{k}
is a rule, then it can be applied in a set in such a way
\{L,x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}
can be rewritten as
\{R_{1}\ldots,R_{k},x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}
.

.
We say that a set of axiomatic linkings
\Lambda\!\!\!\Lambda
on a sequent
\Gamma
is
erasable
if there is a sequence of erasing steps (called
erasing path
) starting from the singleton
\{\mathcal{G}\left({\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\varnothing}\vdash\Gamma::\Lambda\!\!\!\Lambda,\delta^{\Lambda\!\!\!\Lambda}\right)\}
and ending with the singleton containing
\varnothing=\mathcal{G}\left({\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\varnothing}\vdash\varnothing::\varnothing,\delta_{\varnothing}\right)
.

A
slice net
for
\Gamma
is an erasable set of axiomatic linkings
\Lambda\!\!\!\Lambda
.

Remark 31
.

The side conditions of our erasing steps ensures that the connective(s) removed by the step is “ready” to be sequentialized, similarly to how the readiness is defined in
[
53
]
for the slice nets for
\mathsf{MALL}
.

we show an erasing path for the slice net from

Theorem 32
.

Let
\Gamma
be a non-empty sequent.
Then
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{PiL}}\,}\Gamma
iff there is a slice net
\Lambda\!\!\!\Lambda
on
\Gamma
.

Proof.

In
Figure

15
we provide translation from derivations to slice nets defined inductively on the structure of the derivation.
The obtained set of axiomatic linkings is erasable by definition, since each inductive step of the translation preserve erasability.

As for conflict nets, sequentialization for slice nets follows from the existence of a derivation constructed from a given erasing path, since each erasing step corresponds to an application of a sequent rule (with the same name).
∎

\mathsf{MALL}^{1}

.

\mathsf{MALL}^{1}

0.0pt}}}\right\}\!\right\}_{\mathsf{sl}}&\left\{\!\left\{\mathcal{D}_{1}\right\}\!\right\}_{\mathsf{sl}}\cup\left\{\!\left\{\mathcal{D}_{2}\right\}\!\right\}_{\mathsf{sl}}\\[24.0pt]
\lx@intercol\hfil\mbox{with }{\mathsf{r}^{1}}\in\{\invamp,\oplus,\forall,\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}^{\circ},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}^{\circ}\}\quad\mbox{and}\quad{\mathsf{r}^{2}}\in\{\mathop{\otimes},\blacktriangleleft,\blacktriangleleft_{\circ},\mathsf{mix}\}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\nabla\in\{\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}\}\hfil\lx@intercol\end{array}
