Corollary 34
.

The erasing criterion is polynomial in the size of the slice net.

Proof.

The length of a successful erasing path is bound by the size of
\Gamma
, and checking and applying each erasing step can be performed in polinomial time
\mathcal{G}\left(\Lambda\!\!\!\Lambda\right)

∎

Remark 35
.

By case analysis, it is easy to see that erasing steps are locally confluent.

Remark 36
.

The proof translation from derivations to slice nets could be equivalentely defined by letting

\Lambda\!\!\!\Lambda(\mathcal{D})
to be the set of axiomatic linkings on
\Gamma
defined from the conflict net
\left\{\!\left\{\mathcal{D}\right\}\!\right\}_{\mathsf{co}}
as follows:

\left\{\!\left\{\tau(\Lambda)\right\}\!\right\}_{\mathsf{sl}}=\begin{cases}\{{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}\}&\mbox{if ${{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}$ is an axiom link}\\
X_{1}\cup\cdots\cup X_{n}&\mbox{if }\mathcal{D}=\#\left(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}\right)\\
\left\{\bigcup\limits_{x_{1}\in\left\{\!\left\{X_{1}\right\}\!\right\}_{\mathsf{sl}}}\cdots\bigcup\limits_{x_{n}\in\left\{\!\left\{X_{n}\right\}\!\right\}_{\mathsf{sl}}}\left(x_{1}\cup\cdots\cup x_{n}\right)\right\}&\mbox{if }\mathcal{D}=\frown\left(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}\right)\end{cases}

In this translation, it is clear that each conflict node in
\left\{\!\left\{\mathcal{D}\right\}\!\right\}_{\mathsf{co}}
multiplies the elements in the set of linkings, leading to a non-polinomial time transation.

Figure 16:
Rule permutations in
\mathsf{PiL}
.

In this section we prove that conflict nets and slice nets for
\mathsf{PiL}
are proof systems with two distinct canonicity properties called
local
and
strong
canonicity, and they both identify derivations modulo what we refer to as
witness renaming
.

We first introduce three notions of equivalence for derivations in
\mathsf{PiL}
.

Definition 37
.

We call the variable introduced during the proof search by a quantifier rule the
active variable
of that (occurrence of) rule.
The active variable of an existential (resp. universal) quantifier may also be called its
witness

10
10

10

In the general setting of first-order logic, the witness of an existential quantifier could be any term of the language.
However, in
\mathsf{PiL}
witnesses can only be variables because of the simple structure of terms.

(resp.
eigenvariable
), while the active formula of a nominal quantifier may also be called a
fresh name
.
Two derivations
\mathcal{D}_{1}
and
\mathcal{D}_{2}
in
\mathsf{PiL}
are:

•

equivalent modulo active variables
(denoted
\mathcal{D}_{1}\sim_{\mathsf{w}}\mathcal{D}_{2}
) if it is possible to transform
\mathcal{D}_{1}
into
\mathcal{D}_{2}
by changing the active variables of the quantifier rules (and propagating the changes upwards in the derivation);

•

equivalent modulo rule permutations
(denoted
\mathcal{D}_{1}\simeq\mathcal{D}_{2}
) if it is possible to transform
\mathcal{D}_{1}
into
\mathcal{D}_{2}
using all transformations in
Figure

16
;

•

equivalent modulo local rule permutations
(denoted
\mathcal{D}_{1}\approx\mathcal{D}_{2}
) if it is possible to transform
\mathcal{D}_{1}
into
\mathcal{D}_{2}
using the local rule permutations in
Figure

16
.

Moreover, we write
\mathcal{D}_{1}\simeq_{\mathsf{w}}\mathcal{D}_{2}
(resp.
\mathcal{D}_{1}\approx_{\mathsf{w}}\mathcal{D}_{2}
) if they are equivalent modulo rule permutations (resp. local rule permutations) and active variables, that is, if there are derivations
\mathcal{D}_{1}^{\prime}
and
\mathcal{D}_{2}^{\prime\prime}
such that
\mathcal{D}_{1}\sim_{\mathsf{w}}\mathcal{D}_{1}^{\prime}\simeq\mathcal{D}_{2}^{\prime}\sim_{\mathsf{w}}\mathcal{D}_{2}
(resp.
\mathcal{D}_{1}\sim_{\mathsf{w}}\mathcal{D}_{1}^{\prime}\approx\mathcal{D}_{2}^{\prime}\sim_{\mathsf{w}}\mathcal{D}_{2}
).

.

, but the pair of atoms linked by an axiom rule is the same.

to0.0pt{\hss\hbox{$\smash{\lower 2.5pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{ax}\;$}}$}}\vbox{\vbox to0.4pt{\vfill\hbox to55.61346pt{\leaders{\hrule}{\hfill}\kern 0.0pt}\vfill}}\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{$\smash{\lower 2.5pt\hbox{$$}}$}\hss}}\kern 1.43518pt\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{$\kern 0.0pt\hbox{$\vdash\langle x\oc a\rangle,(x\wn a)$}\kern 0.0pt$}}}}}\kern 0.0pt}}\kern 15.81712pt}\kern 1.43518pt\kern-0.7pt\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\hbox{$\smash{\lower 1.8pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\exists\;$}}$}}\vbox{\vbox to1.8pt{\vfill\hbox to87.24771pt{\leaders{\hrule}{\hfill}\kern 0.0pt}\kern 1.0pt\hbox to87.24771pt{\leaders{\hrule}{\hfill}\kern 0.0pt}\vfill}}\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{$\smash{\lower 1.8pt\hbox{$$}}$}\hss}}\kern 1.43518pt\kern-0.7pt\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{$\kern 0.0pt\hbox{$\vdash\exists{x}.\langle x\oc a\rangle,\exists{y}.(y\wn a)$}\kern 0.0pt$}}}}}\kern 0.0pt}}}\quad\sim_{\mathsf{w}}\quad{\vbox{\hbox{\kern 8.97212pt\hbox{\vbox{\hbox{\kern 6.90141pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 9.36938pt\hbox{\vbox{\hbox{\kern 27.35306pt\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{$$}}}\kern 27.35306pt}\kern 1.43518pt\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\hbox{$\smash{\lower 2.5pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{ax}\;$}}$}}\vbox{\vbox to0.4pt{\vfill\hbox to54.70612pt{\leaders{\hrule}{\hfill}\kern 0.0pt}\vfill}}\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{$\smash{\lower 2.5pt\hbox{$$}}$}\hss}}\kern 1.43518pt\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{$\kern 0.0pt\hbox{$\vdash\langle y\oc a\rangle,(y\wn a)$}\kern 0.0pt$}}}}}\kern 0.0pt}}\kern 16.2708pt}\kern 1.43518pt\kern-0.7pt\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\hbox{$\smash{\lower 1.8pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\exists\;$}}$}}\vbox{\vbox to1.8pt{\vfill\hbox to87.24771pt{\leaders{\hrule}{\hfill}\kern 0.0pt}\kern 1.0pt\hbox to87.24771pt{\leaders{\hrule}{\hfill}\kern 0.0pt}\vfill}}\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{$\smash{\lower 1.8pt\hbox{$$}}$}\hss}}\kern 1.43518pt\kern-0.7pt\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{$\kern 0.0pt\hbox{$\vdash\exists{x}.\langle x\oc a\rangle,\exists{y}.(y\wn a)$}\kern 0.0pt$}}}}}\kern 0.0pt}}}\hfill

(13)

We could argue that these two derivations should be not identified because the choice of the witness is part of the information of the proof.
In a boarder sense, it may be useful to not identify a proof using a very elementary witness with a proof using a quite complex one.
However, because of the quite limited syntax of atoms (terms) in
\mathsf{PiL}
, witness for quanfitiers can only be varibles.
Therefore, as soon as the choice of witness do not change the pairs of atoms which are mated by the
\mathsf{ax}
-rules in the derivation, such a choice can be considered irrelevant, especially if the choice of the witness of a
\nabla_{\mathsf{pop}}
depends on varible previously stored by a
\nabla_{\mathsf{load}}
, which is arbitrary because of
\alpha
-equivalence.
Note that the two sub-derivations of the
\sim_{\mathsf{w}}
-equivalent derivations in
Equation

13
made only of the
\mathsf{ax}
-rules are not
\sim_{\mathsf{w}}
-equivalent.
That is

{\vbox{\hbox{\kern 9.36938pt\hbox{\vbox{\hbox{\kern 27.80673pt\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{$$}}}\kern 27.80673pt}\kern 1.43518pt\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\hbox{$\smash{\lower 2.5pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{ax}\;$}}$}}\vbox{\vbox to0.4pt{\vfill\hbox to55.61346pt{\leaders{\hrule}{\hfill}\kern 0.0pt}\vfill}}\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{$\smash{\lower 2.5pt\hbox{$$}}$}\hss}}\kern 1.43518pt\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{$\kern 0.0pt\hbox{$\vdash\langle x\oc a\rangle,(x\wn a)$}\kern 0.0pt$}}}}}\kern 0.0pt}}}\;\not\sim_{\mathsf{w}}\;{\vbox{\hbox{\kern 9.36938pt\hbox{\vbox{\hbox{\kern 27.35306pt\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{$$}}}\kern 27.35306pt}\kern 1.43518pt\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\hbox{$\smash{\lower 2.5pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{ax}\;$}}$}}\vbox{\vbox to0.4pt{\vfill\hbox to54.70612pt{\leaders{\hrule}{\hfill}\kern 0.0pt}\vfill}}\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{$\smash{\lower 2.5pt\hbox{$$}}$}\hss}}\kern 1.43518pt\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{$\kern 0.0pt\hbox{$\vdash\langle y\oc a\rangle,(y\wn a)$}\kern 0.0pt$}}}}}\kern 0.0pt}}}
.

However, the choice of active variables may change the pair of atoms linked by the
\mathsf{ax}
-rules.
For an example, see
Equation

14
below, where we show two non
\sim_{\mathsf{w}}
-equivalent derivations in which we trace the occurrences of atoms in the derivation to show how the choice of the active variables changes the pairs of atoms linked by the
\mathsf{ax}
-rules.

(14)

We conclude by proving our the canonicity results.

Definition 39
.

Two conflict nets
\tau(\Lambda)_{1}
and
\tau(\Lambda)_{2}
are
the same
(denoted
\tau(\Lambda)_{1}=\tau(\Lambda)_{2}
) if they are isomorphic co-tree, that is, if there is a bijection between the nodes of
\tau(\Lambda)_{1}
and
\tau(\Lambda)_{2}
that preserves the structure of the tree.

For slice nets
\Lambda\!\!\!\Lambda_{1}
and
\Lambda\!\!\!\Lambda_{2}
are
the same
(denoted
\Lambda\!\!\!\Lambda_{1}=\Lambda\!\!\!\Lambda_{2}
) if they are the same set of linkings.

Lemma 40
.

Let
\tau(\Lambda)
be a conflict net on
\Gamma
such that
\tau(\Lambda)
sequetializes to
\mathcal{D}_{\tau(\Lambda)}
.
If
\tau(\Lambda)\rightarrow^{*}\tau(\Lambda)^{\prime}
,
then
\tau(\Lambda)^{\prime}
sequentializes to a
\mathcal{D}_{\tau(\Lambda)^{\prime}}
such that
\mathcal{D}_{\tau(\Lambda)^{\prime}}\approx_{\mathsf{w}}\mathcal{D}_{\tau(\Lambda)}
.

Proof.

It suffices to check that each critical pair of coalescence steps on deductive
co-trees converges.
For this, we should consider the derivations labeling each link modulo the proof equivalence generated by local rule permutations
Figure

16
.

The most convoluted case is the one for the pair
\#/\#
, for which we use the same argument in
[
42
]
, remarking that the base case of induction presents no problems in our setting (where we have the additional information of the dualizers) because of the associativity of the join operator on dualizers.
Note that critical pairs with non-trivial confluence (i.e., non-local) are the ones where the rule
\with
interacts with quantifiers, and the ones of the form
\mathsf{mix}/\mathsf{mix}
and
\blacktriangleleft_{\circ}/\blacktriangleleft_{\circ}
.
Details are provided in
Appendix

B
.
∎

Theorem 41
.

Let
\mathcal{D}
and
\mathcal{D}^{\prime}
be two derivations.
Then, the following hold:

1.

\mathcal{D}\approx_{\mathsf{w}}\mathcal{D}^{\prime}
iff
\left\{\!\left\{\mathcal{D}\right\}\!\right\}_{\mathsf{co}}=\left\{\!\left\{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}\right\}\!\right\}_{\mathsf{co}}
.

2.

\mathcal{D}\simeq_{\mathsf{w}}\mathcal{D}^{\prime}
iff
\left\{\!\left\{\mathcal{D}\right\}\!\right\}_{\mathsf{sl}}=\left\{\!\left\{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}\right\}\!\right\}_{\mathsf{sl}}
.

Proof.

It suffices to consider the case analysis given by the rule permutations in
Figure

16
as done in
[
52
]
for conflict nets, and in
[
56
]
for slice nets.

1.

For
\approx_{\mathsf{w}}
it follows from the definition of
\left\{\!\left\{\cdot\right\}\!\right\}_{\mathsf{co}}
and by
Lemma

40
.
The only new cases with respect to
[
52
]
are given by the local rule permutation changing
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{pop}}+\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}}
into a
\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\mathsf{pop}}+\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}}
(the permutation boxed in
Figure

16
), and the definition of equivalence modulo fresh names.

2.

Similarly, for
\simeq_{\mathsf{w}}
it follows from the definition of
\left\{\!\left\{\cdot\right\}\!\right\}_{\mathsf{sl}}
and by
Remark

35
.

∎

7
Processes as Formulas

In this section we show how
\mathsf{PiL}
can be used as a logical framework in which we can intepret proofs as execution trees in the
\pi
-calculus.

First we provide a translation from processes to formulas in
\mathsf{PiL}
and show that the logical implication in
\mathsf{PiL}
captures the structural congruence in the
\pi
-calculus.
According to
[
64
]
, the absence of this property suggests that the logical framework may lack a robust design.

Notation 42
.

Because of the monoidal laws, we consider generalized
n
-ary versions (with
n>0
) of the additive connectives
\mathop{\oplus}
and
\with
, which are more convenient for the translation of processes.
Their inference rules are defined as expected:
the
n
-ary version of the
\mathop{\oplus}
-rule keeps a unique component of the
n
-ary disjunction,
while the
n
-ary version of the
\with
-rule has
n
premises containing only one of the component of the
n
-ary conjunction, and a copy of the context.

Definition 43

(Processes-as-Formulas)
.

The formula
\left\llbracket P\right\rrbracket
associated to a process
P
is inductively defined as follows:

\begin{array}[]{r@{\;=\;}l@{\qquad}r@{\;=\;}l}\left\llbracket\mathsf{Nil}\right\rrbracket=\circ\qquad\left\llbracket P\;|\;Q\right\rrbracket&\left\llbracket P\right\rrbracket\invamp\left\llbracket Q\right\rrbracket&\left\llbracket(\nu x)(P)\right\rrbracket&\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}{x}.\left\llbracket P\right\rrbracket\\
\left\llbracket x!\langle y\rangle.P\right\rrbracket&\langle x\oc y\rangle\blacktriangleleft\left\llbracket P\right\rrbracket&\left\llbracket x?(y).P\right\rrbracket&\exists{y}.\!\left((x\wn y)\blacktriangleleft\left\llbracket P\right\rrbracket\right)\\
\left\llbracket x\triangleright\left\{\ell:P_{\ell}\right\}_{\ell\in L}\right\rrbracket&\bigoplus\limits_{\ell\in L}{\left((x\wn\ell)\blacktriangleleft\left\llbracket P_{\ell}\right\rrbracket\right)}&\left\llbracket x\triangleleft\left\{\ell:P_{\ell}\right\}_{\ell\in L}\right\rrbracket&\bigwith\limits_{\ell\in L}{\left(\langle x\oc\ell\rangle\blacktriangleleft\left\llbracket P_{\ell}\right\rrbracket\right)}\end{array}

(15)

We denote by
\left\lfloor\!\left\lfloor P\right\rfloor\!\right\rfloor
the sequent obtained by recursively removing all top-level
\invamp
-connectives and nominal quantifiers from the sequent, as well as units and unary additive connectives. If the obtained sequent is empty, then we let
\left\lfloor\!\left\lfloor P\right\rfloor\!\right\rfloor=\circ
.

Corollary 44
.

Let
P
and
Q
be processes.
If
P\equiv Q
, then
\left\llbracket Q\right\rrbracket\multimapboth\left\llbracket P\right\rrbracket
.

Notation 45
.

When translating the processes
x!\langle y\rangle=x!\langle y\rangle.\mathsf{Nil}
(and similarly for
x?(y)
), we will simply write
\left\llbracket x!\langle y\rangle.\mathsf{Nil}\right\rrbracket=\langle x\oc y\rangle
since
\left\llbracket x!\langle y\rangle.\mathsf{Nil}\right\rrbracket=\langle x\oc y\rangle\blacktriangleleft\circ
is logically equivalent to
\langle x\oc y\rangle
.

Remark 46
.

For a counter-example of processes which are not
\equiv
-equivalent, but whose corresponding formulas are
\multimapboth
-equivalent, consider the process where fresh new name is chosen before a choice, and the one in which a fresh name is chosen after a choice.

\hfill P=(\nu x)\left(x\triangleleft\left\{\ell:P_{\ell}\right\}_{\ell\in L}\right)\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad Q=x\triangleleft\left\{\ell:(\nu x)P_{\ell}\right\}_{\ell\in L}\hfill

(16)

These processes are not equivalent modulo the structural equivalence
\equiv
provided in literature
[
85
,
32
]
, which is the same as the one we provide in
Figure

2
.

It is worth noticing that Milner’s original
\pi
-calculus includes the structural equivalence in the top of
Equation

17
, while, at the best of our knowledge, the literature on the
\pi
-calculus as presented in this paper (that is, as in
[
85
,
32
]
) does not include the corresponding structural equivalence in the bottom of
Equation

17
, required to capture similar interactions between choices and restriction.

\hfill\begin{array}[]{c@{\quad\steq\quad}c}(\nu x)\left(A+B\right)\hfil\quad\equiv&(\nu x)A+(\nu x)B\\
\hline\cr\hline\cr x\triangleleft\left\{\ell:(\nu y)P_{\ell}\right\}_{\ell\in L}\hfil\quad\equiv&(\nu y)\left(x\triangleleft\left\{\ell:P_{\ell}\right\}_{\ell\in L}\right)\\
x\triangleright\left\{\ell:(\nu y)P_{\ell}\right\}_{\ell\in L}\hfil\quad\equiv&(\nu y)\left(x\triangleright\left\{\ell:P_{\ell}\right\}_{\ell\in L}\right)\end{array}\hfill

(17)

This rises an interesting question on why those structural equivalences have not being used in the literature, even if the two processes in
Equation

16
have the same behavior with respect to the results in session types.

As shown in detail in
[
8
]
, it is possible to associate to each execution tree of a process
P
to an open derivation in
\mathsf{PiL}
of a formula
\left\llbracket P\right\rrbracket
, therefore to characterize deadlock-freedom in terms of derivability in
\mathsf{PiL}
.
We report here only a sketch of the proof of this result.

Theorem 47

(
[
8
]
)
.

Let
P
be a process.

1.

If
P
is a deadlock-free, then
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{PiL}}\,}\left\llbracket P\right\rrbracket
.

2.

If
P
is race-free, then
P
is deadlock-fre iff
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{PiL}}\,}\left\llbracket P\right\rrbracket
.

Sketch of proof.

If
P
is deadlock-free, then each (maximal) execution tree
\mathcal{T}
of
P
has leaves
\mathsf{Nil}
.
Since terms are considered up-to structural equivalence, we can assume without loss of generality that no child of a process
P
contains more occurrences of
\mathsf{Nil}
than
P
.
This can be obtained by orienting the structural equivalence
P\;|\;\mathsf{Nil}\equiv P
in the natural way.

For each such tree, we define a derivation
\left\llbracket\mathcal{T}\right\rrbracket
by induction on the structure of
\mathcal{T}
as shown in
Figure

17
.

Item

1
follows by definition.
To prove
Item

2
, we show that we can transform a derivation of a formula
\left\llbracket P\right\rrbracket
into a derivation made of blocks of rules as in
Figure

17
using rule permutations from
Figure

16
.
We conclude by remarking that it suffices to check a unique derivation because when
P
is deadlock-free, then all derivations of
\left\llbracket P\right\rrbracket
are equivalent with respect to the interleaving relation defined in
Figure

3
.
∎

Remark 48
.

Certain works on
\pi
-calculus (e.g.,
[
80
]
) restrict communication and selection on restricted channels (i.e., communication or selection on a channel
y
can be performed only if
y
is bound by a
\nu
).
To capture such a restriction it would be sufficient to require that an
\mathsf{ax}
-rule with conclusion
\langle x\oc y\rangle
and
(x\wn y)
can be applied only if the
x
is bounded by a
\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}
in a sequent occurring in the derivation below the rule.

The canonicity result on proof nets with respect to the sequent calculus allows us to provide canonical representatives of execution trees modulo inteleaving.
To prove this result not only for deadlock-free processes, we extend the syntax of proof nets to include
non-logical axioms
to model open premises of a derivation.

Theorem 50
.

Two execution trees of a processes
P
are equivalent modulo interleaving (resp. local interleaving)
iff
they can be represented by the same open slice net (resp. open conflict net).

Proof.

We associate each execution tree
\mathcal{T}
the slice net
\left\{\!\left\{\mathcal{T}\right\}\!\right\}_{\mathsf{sl}}
by combining the translations in
Figure

17
and
Figure

15
(plus the special case for open premises defined in
Definition

49
).
If
\mathcal{T}\sim\mathcal{T}^{\prime}
, then
\left\llbracket\mathcal{T}\right\rrbracket\simeq\left\llbracket\mathcal{T}^{\prime}\right\rrbracket
; therefore
\left\{\!\left\{\mathcal{T}\right\}\!\right\}_{\mathsf{sl}}=\left\{\!\left\{\mathcal{T}^{\prime}\right\}\!\right\}_{\mathsf{sl}}
by
Theorem

41
.
The result for local interleaving is similar.
∎

Corollary 51
.

A process
P
is race-free iff there is a unique possible slice net for
\left\llbracket P\right\rrbracket
.

8
Conclusion and Future Works

In this paper we presented
\mathsf{PiL}
, an extension of first-order multiplicative-additive linear logic in which non-commutativity is not obtained by considering sequents as lists of formulas (as in
[
1
,
79
,
31
]
), but rather including a non-commutative binary connective, as in Retoré’s
\mathsf{Pomset}
logic
[
75
,
76
]
or Guglielmi’s
\mathsf{BV}

[
40
]
.
We have shown that by requiring such non-commutative connective to also be non-associative, we can design sequent calculus in which the
\mathsf{cut}
-rule is admissible.
We also provided proof nets for this logic with a polynomial-time correctness criterion (that is, proof nets form a proof system in the sense of
[
24
]
), polynomial-time sequentialization and proof translation, and we showed that proof nets provide canonical representatives of derivations modulo local rule permutations.
Note that our result is stronger than what needed to define proof nets (both conflict and slice nets) for
\mathsf{MALL}^{1}
, addressing a question left open in the literature. Moreover, it could be possible to define both conflict and slice ‘witness nets’ for
\mathsf{PiL}
(and then for
\mathsf{MALL}^{1}
) by including in the initial data of the proof net the information of a specific witness map instead of the initial witness map.

Characerization of deadlock-freedom.

In
[
8
]
we have shown that each derivation in
\mathsf{PiL}
of the formula
\left\llbracket P\right\rrbracket
can be interpreted as a execution tree of the process
P
of the
\pi
-calculus (defined as in
[
85
,
32
]
).
In the same paper, we used such a correspondence to show that (finite) deadlock-freedom and race-free processes can be characterized in terms of derivability in
\mathsf{PiL}
.
To remove the race-free condition, we should be able to reason over all possible proof-search attempts, which has an exponential blowup because of interleaving.
We are currently studying the possibility of reducing this blowup by using slice nets, allowing us to quantify over sets of linkings which may be valid slice nets instead of all possible “maximal open derivations”.

Extensions of
\mathsf{PiL}
with fixpoints.

In this work, we have studied the recursion-free fragment of the
\pi
-calculus, but we foresee the possibility of modeling the following three main approaches for the definition of infinite behaviors (see
[
22
]
for a comparison of their expressive power).

Replication
(resp.
iteration
) could be modeled using the modality
why-not
(resp.
flag
) defined as fixpoint of the equation
\wn A=A\invamp(\wn A)
(resp.

Proof systems capturing these operators should include rules allowing the definition of correct non-wellfounded derivations as in, e.g.,
[
16
,
4
,
9
]
.
An interesting challenge will be to find a suitable syntax for infinitary proof nets for these systems aiming at proof canonicity rather than to well-behavior with respect to cut-elimination as in
[
26
,
25
]
.

Coherent spaces for
\mathsf{NML}
.

As a consequence of
Theorem

17
and cut-elimination, we have that
\mathsf{NML}
embeds in
\mathsf{BV}
, therefore
\mathsf{NML}
embeds in
\mathsf{Pomset}
.
Since
\mathsf{Pomset}
admits a semantics in terms of coherent spaces
[
75
,
76
]
, it should be possible to characterize the class of
\mathsf{NML}
theorems inside
\mathsf{Pomset}
, and use this logic to study sequential algorithms
[
74
,
28
,
29
]
.

Applications to concurrent programming languages.

This paper represents the first step in the definition of a novel paradigm allowing to intepret proofs as execution trees, and using proof equivalence to identify execution trees differing from interleaving concurrency, allowing for the developments of new methods complementary to the ones based session types.

In
[
8
]
we have shown that deadlock-freedom can be characterized in terms of derivability in
\mathsf{PiL}
, providing the first completeness result for choreographic programming with respect to recursion-free deadlock-freedom.
This was an open question in the literature, and the main difficulty of proving this result was due to syntactic limitations of session types in presence of key features such as name mobility or cyclic dependencies.
By developing a theory of
\mathsf{PiL}
with fixpoints, we expect to be able to extend this result to the full
\pi
-calculus.

We plan to study applications of our framework such as the definition of a notion of orthogonality for formulas based on the existence of (open) proof nets which could be completed by set of axioms connecting them (see the notion of module in
[
14
,
7
]
).
This could be used to characterize the
testing preorders

[
27
,
43
,
19
]
, thus designing verification tools whose efficiency relies on the low complexity of the proof net correctness criterion, combined with the fact that a single proof net can encode an exponential number of equivalent executions.

Moreover, our methodology is complementary to algebraic methods which, to the best of our knowledge, currently lack of methods to model name mobility and restrictions.
This because these features are strongly tight to quantification, and modeling quantification has proven to be a complex task in algebraic settings:
while Boolean and Heyting algebras provide straightforward algebraic models for classical and intuitionistic propositional logic respectively, the algebraic structures modeling first-order classical logic have only recently been studied (see
[
20
]
).

Towards a semantics for sequentiality.

In this paper we used the non-associative connective
\blacktriangleleft
to model a special form of sequentiality, the prefix operator, but we consider extending this work to sequent calculi using graphical connectives (in the sense of
[
3
]
) to model more complex pattern of interactions as done in
[
6
]
, as well as study deep inference systems to recover associativity of the sequential operator – thus more similar to the systems studied in
[
21
,
48
,
45
]
.

.

In
\mathsf{NML}
we have the same connectives
\invamp
and

\mathsf{BV}

\mathsf{BV}

Case
{\mathsf{r}}/\#
with
{\mathsf{r}}\in\{\exists,\forall,\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}},\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\circ},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\circ}\}
:

\begin{array}[]{ccc}\#(a_{1},\dots,a_{l},b_{1},\dots,b_{k},c)&\to&\#(\#(a_{1},\dots,a_{l}),\#(b_{1},\dots,b_{k},c))\\
\downarrow&&\downarrow\\
\#(a_{1},\dots,a_{l},b_{1},\dots,b_{k},c^{\prime})&\to&\#(\#(a_{1},\dots,a_{l}),\#(b_{1},\dots,b_{k},c^{\prime}))\end{array}

Where either

–

{\mathsf{r}}\in\{\forall,\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\circ},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\circ},\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\mathsf{load}}\}
, thus

c=\Gamma,A
,
c^{\prime}=\Gamma,\mathord{\text{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{\rotatebox[origin={c}]{180.0}{$\mathsf{Q}$}}}}{x}.A
, and
\delta_{c^{\prime}}=\delta_{c}
; or

–

{\mathsf{r}}\in\{\exists,\mathord{\text{\char 200\relax}}_{\mathsf{pop}},\mathord{\text{\char 223\relax}}_{\mathsf{pop}}\}
, thus

c=\Gamma,A
,
c^{\prime}=\Gamma,\exists{x}.A
and
\delta_{c^{\prime}}=\delta_{c}\setminus\{x\}
.

The derivation labelling the link in the bottom-right corner of the diagram is the same, independently of the sequence of coalescence steps.

•

Case
\mathsf{mix}/\mathsf{mix}
:

if this case applies, then the co-tree has a
\frown
-node
x
with leaves on which only
(\mathsf{mix})
can be applied to merge some of them.
In particular,
x
must have at least three leaves
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}
,
{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{b}}}
and
{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}{c}}}
such that, without loss of generaltity, a
(\mathsf{mix})
can be appliet to merge
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}
and
{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{b}}}
, or to merge
{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{b}}}
and
{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}{c}}}
.
Let
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{ab}}
be the link obtained by applying a
(\mathsf{mix})
step to merge
{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{a}}}
and
{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{b}}}
.
To conclude it suffices to remark that we can always find a continuation of the coalescence path containing such step
(\mathsf{mix})
which also contain another step
(\mathsf{mix})
merging
{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}{c}}}
and the link obtained by applying coalescence steps involving
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{ab}}
.
This follows from the fact that the side condition of the step
(\mathsf{mix})
implies that, if exists,
the least common ancestor (in the forest of
\Gamma
) of two formulas from two links which could be have been merged using a step
(\mathsf{mix})
must be a
\invamp
.
Thus, under the conditio that
\tau(\Lambda)
is a proof net, once we cannot apply any more coalescence step to a link obtained from
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{ab}}
, we are still able to apply a
(\mathsf{mix})
step to merge it with
{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}{c}}}
.

•

Case
\blacktriangleleft_{\circ}/\blacktriangleleft_{\circ}
:
similar to the previous case.

Finally, we have the following special additional cases, in which the dualizer is not the same, but the proof nets are.

•

Case
